articles.summary: South Korea Sets Five-Year Push to Double Semiconductor Production, Seeks U.S. Investment for AI Supply Chains  Spherical Insights
articles.full_text:
South Korea is stepping up its semiconductor expansion and AI strategy as it seeks to increase chip-production capabilities, attract U.S. investment and build supply chains that are more resilient to external disruptions.
South Korea is entering a new phase of semiconductor expansion as artificial intelligence drives demand for advanced computing, memory and data-centre infrastructure. On September 23, 2026, President Lee Jae Myung announced that the country aims to double semiconductor production capabilities within five years while seeking U.S. investment and stronger AI supply chains resilient to external shocks. The announcement comes as semiconductor exports reach record levels, with August exports rising 209% year over year to $46.65 billion, according to South Korea’s Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources. The strategy extends beyond production growth, focusing on AI infrastructure and supply-chain resilience. With Samsung Electronics and SK hynix central to South Korea’s semiconductor industry, the expansion could influence global chip capacity, investment and AI supply chains.
South Korea’s Semiconductor Industry Enters a New Growth Phase
South Korea remains a major global semiconductor manufacturing hub, particularly in memory chips, with Samsung Electronics and SK hynix holding strong positions in DRAM and high-bandwidth memory (HBM). HBM has become increasingly important as AI accelerators require faster, higher-capacity memory for training and inference workloads. SK hynix reported that it began mass shipments of HBM4 in the second quarter of 2026, while Samsung is also expanding its HBM4 business as AI infrastructure investment accelerates.
The strength of this segment is also visible in South Korea’s trade performance. In August 2026, semiconductor exports reached a record $46.65 billion, rising 209% year over year, with demand supported by AI infrastructure investment from major hyperscalers. Semiconductors therefore remain central to the country’s export economy, while rising demand for advanced memory is increasing the importance of domestic production capacity. South Korea’s broader semiconductor strategy is consequently focused not only on maintaining its memory leadership but also on expanding manufacturing capacity, supporting advanced technologies and strengthening supply-chain resilience.

South Korea’s Double-Production Plan: What Happened?
At the Korea Investment Summit in New York on September 23, 2026, President Lee Jae Myung announced that South Korea would double its semiconductor production capabilities within five years by expanding a chip-production hub. He linked the plan to the country’s three megaprojects, launched earlier in 2026 to develop a semiconductor cluster and other AI facilities. The government also plans to establish a Future Fund to support industrial infrastructure and talent development, while pursuing conditions intended to attract additional global investment. Lee said the strategy would also focus on building critical AI supply chains that are less vulnerable to external shocks.
Why Is South Korea Targeting Higher Semiconductor Production?
Rising AI computing needs are making advanced chips, memory, data centres, and secure supply chains increasingly important to South Korea’s technology strategy.
Rising AI Chip Demand
AI training and inference require increasingly powerful processors and high-performance memory. Expanding domestic semiconductor capacity can help South Korea respond to this growing demand while supporting its broader AI ambitions.
HBM and Advanced Memory Growth
HBM has become a critical component of AI computing because it enables high-speed data movement between processors and memory. South Korea is therefore prioritizing next-generation memory technologies to maintain technological strength as AI workloads become more demanding.
Global Supply-Chain Resilience
Semiconductor production depends on complex international networks for equipment, materials and components. Increasing domestic capacity and developing supporting industries can reduce exposure to disruptions and strengthen Korea’s position within global supply chains.
Growing Data-Center Infrastructure
AI expansion requires large-scale computing infrastructure, creating additional demand for processors, memory, networking and supporting technologies. South Korea’s government has outlined plans for 8.4 GW of AI data-center capacity, with phased operations planned from 2029.
Strategic Technology Competition
Semiconductor leadership is increasingly connected to national competitiveness in AI and other advanced technologies. South Korea is strengthening its ecosystem through support for next-generation semiconductors, AI infrastructure and domestic technology development as competition intensifies globally.
How Is AI Changing South Korea’s Semiconductor Strategy?
AI data centres require powerful GPUs, AI accelerators and high-performance computing systems supported by HBM and advanced packaging. As AI workloads expand, demand is increasing for memory with greater bandwidth and capacity, making advanced semiconductor manufacturing more important. This is pushing South Korea to strengthen AI infrastructure and chip capabilities across processors, memory, packaging and data-centre technologies.
Samsung and SK hynix: What Role Could Korea’s Chip Giants Play?
Samsung Electronics
Samsung combines memory, foundry and advanced semiconductor manufacturing within its chip business. In Q2 2026, its Memory Business reported record quarterly revenue and expanded HBM4 sales, while it also shipped HBM4E samples to major customers. Samsung and Broadcom additionally announced a collaboration spanning memory, foundry and advanced packaging, with an estimated value of more than $200 billion through 2030.
SK hynix
SK hynix is strengthening its position in HBM, AI memory, NAND and advanced packaging. The company reported Q2 2026 revenue of KRW 79.32 trillion and began HBM4 mass shipments during the quarter. It also announced KRW 100 trillion of investment in Cheongju, including KRW 80 trillion for the M17 NAND fab and KRW 20 trillion for the P&T7 advanced-packaging facility.

Supply-Chain Security Is Becoming a Strategic Priority
Semiconductor production depends on a broad network of materials, equipment, components and manufacturing facilities. South Korea is therefore developing multiple regional production and support hubs to diversify capacity and strengthen the resilience of its semiconductor value chain.

South Korea’s next semiconductor cycle is likely to center on HBM, advanced DRAM, 3D memory architectures, advanced packaging and AI accelerators. Taiwan remains important to advanced foundry manufacturing, while U.S. companies contribute strongly to AI processors, chip design and semiconductor equipment.

articles.summary: US, South Korea and Japan reaffirm North Korea denuclearization  streamlinefeed.co.ke
articles.full_text:
The top diplomats of the United States, South Korea and Japan reaffirmed their commitment to the complete denuclearization of North Korea on Monday, meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York and calling on Pyongyang to return to dialogue.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun and Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi agreed to maintain a firm deterrence posture while coordinating efforts to preserve peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula through dialogue and diplomacy, South Korea's Foreign Ministry said. A joint statement released by the US State Department said the path to dialogue remains open and called on North Korea to resume talks.
What the joint statement said
The ministers reaffirmed their commitment to denuclearization in accordance with UN Security Council resolutions and pledged to prevent illicit revenue generation that supports Pyongyang's nuclear and ballistic missile programmes. They welcomed the work of the Multilateral Sanctions Monitoring Team, which tracks implementation of UN sanctions, and efforts to counter North Korean cyber threats.
Anadolu Agency reported that the statement also welcomed an alert on North Korean IT workers issued by like minded countries, committed to a new trilateral consultation on economic security, and endorsed implementation of a July 7 memorandum to accelerate small modular reactor deployments in other countries under high standards of safety, security and nonproliferation. The statement reiterated US defence commitments to South Korea and Japan, including nuclear forces, and emphasised peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait.
- Meeting: trilateral foreign ministers' meeting on the UN General Assembly sidelines, September 21.
- Core position: complete denuclearization of North Korea under UN Security Council resolutions.
- Dialogue: the path to dialogue remains open, with a call on Pyongyang to resume talks.
- Security: US extended deterrence commitments reaffirmed, including nuclear forces.
Deterrence and dialogue in tension
The statement's importance lies in its attempt to hold two positions at once. The three governments are strengthening deterrence and sanctions monitoring while saying diplomacy remains available. This is not new language. NK News reported that the statement largely echoed the allies' position from their September 2025 meeting, when they agreed to maintain deterrence and close coordination while upholding denuclearization.
That continuity matters because North Korea has hardened its own position. NK News reported that Pyongyang has declared its nuclear status absolute and that leader Kim Jong Un has repeatedly said the country will not give up nuclear weapons. Pyongyang has left open the possibility of talks with Washington only if the United States accepts what it calls irreversible nuclear status. The gap between that demand and the allies' denuclearization goal remains the central obstacle.
South Korea's incremental proposal
Within the alliance, South Korea is signalling a more incremental approach. NK News reported that President Lee Jae Myung, in an interview with The New York Times published Monday, argued that pursuing denuclearization under current circumstances would accomplish nothing and suggested a possible trade off in which sanctions relief is exchanged for freezing development of additional nuclear weapons and intercontinental ballistic missile technology.
That idea does not replace the trilateral commitment to complete denuclearization, but it shows the practical debate inside Seoul. If North Korea will not negotiate full disarmament, an interim freeze could limit the growth of its arsenal. The United States and Japan have not endorsed that formulation in this statement, and the joint text still anchors the alliance to complete denuclearization.
What the meeting does not resolve
The trilateral statement does not bridge the gap with Pyongyang. It restates principles, welcomes sanctions monitoring and keeps the door open, but it does not offer new incentives sufficient to change North Korea's declared position. It also does not resolve whether Washington might pursue a separate leader level diplomacy, as President Donald Trump has continued to signal interest in another meeting with Kim.
NK News reported that a potential meeting on the sidelines of November's Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China remains possible, although Pyongyang has shown little urgency about engaging. Trump's outreach followed Washington's decision to shorten the annual Ulchi Freedom Shield military exercise, but North Korea has indicated that changes to the broader US military posture and sanctions regime would be important to renewed engagement.
Why this matters beyond the peninsula
The statement also connects Korean Peninsula security to wider regional issues. By reaffirming peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait and opposing unilateral changes to the status quo, the three governments link North Korea policy to the broader Indo Pacific security environment. The economic security provisions, including supply chain early warning systems and small modular reactor cooperation, show that the trilateral agenda is expanding beyond pure military coordination.
The verified outcome of Monday's meeting is therefore continuity rather than breakthrough. The United States, South Korea and Japan remain aligned on denuclearization, deterrence and sanctions, while North Korea continues to reject that framework. The next test will be whether the allies can develop an interim diplomacy that limits Pyongyang's nuclear growth without conceding permanent nuclear status, and whether any leader level channel can move from speculation to negotiation.

South Korean President Lee Jae-myung stood before investors in New York on September 23 and laid out a plan that amounts to the country’s biggest industrial bet in decades: double semiconductor production capacity within five years.
The numbers behind the pledge
Samsung Electronics and SK hynix have committed a combined investment exceeding 800 trillion won, roughly $518 to $520 billion. That money is earmarked for four new memory fabrication plants, supplier networks, and the infrastructure needed to keep them running.
When you layer in spending on AI data centers and the government’s other two “megaprojects,” total investment is expected to surpass 880 trillion to 1 quadrillion won.
Samsung and SK hynix together already account for about two-thirds of global memory chip production, so doubling their output isn’t just a South Korean story. It’s a global supply story.
President Lee referred to Samsung Chairman Lee Jae-yong and SK Group Chairman Chey Tae-won as “national heroes” for their investment commitments.

Where the fabs will go
The five-year target was first detailed on June 29, 2026, as part of three megaprojects focusing on semiconductors, physical AI, and AI data centers. The September summit in New York served as the international sales pitch for the same vision.

articles.title: South Korea’s Lee urges sanctions relief in exchange for North Korean nuclear freeze - stripes.com
articles.summary: South Korea’s Lee urges sanctions relief in exchange for North Korean nuclear freeze  stripes.com
articles.full_text:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung is urging Washington to ease sanctions on North Korea in exchange for freezing its nuclear and missile programs, an approach one North Korea expert called the “least bad option” for slowing the expansion of Pyongyang’s arsenal.
Lee said in an interview published Monday in the New York Times that there is “significant value in a trade-off between sanctions” and efforts to halt the North’s development of additional nuclear weapons and ballistic missiles.
He argued that sanctions are not “particularly effective” and that insisting on denuclearization before making progress “guarantees that nothing will be accomplished,” according to the Times.
Lee also said President Donald Trump is the only leader capable of bringing North Korean leader Kim Jong Un back to negotiations.
Trump told reporters last month that Kim had responded “very positively” to his overtures for dialogue. Trump said Aug. 19 that he planned to meet Kim later this year.
The Wall Street Journal previously reported that Trump was seeking a face-to-face meeting with Kim during an anticipated trip to APEC — the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum in Shenzhen, China.
Lee warned that allowing North Korea’s weapons programs to continue unchecked could result in a substantially larger arsenal and eventually increase the risk of Pyongyang exporting nuclear weapons.
“Our estimates suggest that North Korea is now capable of producing, or may already be producing, an additional 10 to 20 nuclear weapons each year,” he told the Times. “Once it believes it has accumulated enough nuclear weapons and missiles to guarantee its survival, it will be tempted to export them to make money.”
Lee warned: “That will be a truly dangerous moment.”
The White House did not immediately respond to an after-hours request for comment Tuesday in Washington.
Lee’s proposal reflects the reality that persuading Pyongyang to surrender its nuclear arsenal is increasingly unlikely, said Andrei Lankov, a professor at Kookmin University in Seoul who specializes in North Korean affairs.
“North Koreans have always been determined to remain nuclear,” he told Stars and Stripes by phone Wednesday. “Their experience of decades of negotiations has demonstrated that no amount of pressure, no amount of compensation or reward will persuade them to surrender their nuclear weapons.”
The “least bad option,” Lankov said, is to accept that North Korea is unlikely to denuclearize and “try to freeze the situation in its current shape.”
Lankov cautioned, however, that securing such an agreement would be difficult.
“North Koreans are likely to demand a lot in exchange for the agreement to freeze their program,” he said.
North Korea’s improving economy and support from China and Russia mean Pyongyang would probably demand significantly more in exchange for concessions than it did during negotiations with Washington seven years ago, Lankov said.
Trump and Kim met in Hanoi in 2019 for their second summit. North Korea offered to dismantle its Yongbyon nuclear complex in exchange for sanctions relief, but the two sides failed to reach an agreement.
Lee, who took office in June 2025, has advocated for improving relations with North Korea and reducing tensions on the Korean Peninsula.
Pyongyang, however, has given no public indication that it is prepared to resume negotiations with either Seoul or Washington. It has continued to test weapons and fortify its defenses along the inter-Korean border.

articles.title: Foreign Capital Exodus Meets Earnings Upgrades: South Korea's Memory Chip Sector at a 4.7x P/E Crossroads - finance.biggo.com
articles.summary: Foreign Capital Exodus Meets Earnings Upgrades: South Korea's Memory Chip Sector at a 4.7x P/E Crossroads  finance.biggo.com
articles.full_text:
South Korea's semiconductor market is caught in a rare pricing divergence: foreign ownership has slid to an extreme historical low, while analysts continue to revise earnings estimates upward. The gap between the two has pushed the memory chip sector's valuation to a critical inflection point—whether 4.7x forward earnings represents deep undervaluation or a classic cyclical peak trap remains unanswered by the market.
According to Goldman Sachs data, foreign ownership of South Korea's KOSPI semiconductor sector has fallen to 49.1%, sitting 2.1 standard deviations below its historical average. This positioning loss is not evenly distributed but almost entirely concentrated in the memory chip space. Excluding Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and SK Hynix (000660.KS), foreign ownership levels in the remaining constituents are close to historical norms.
In other words, foreign investors are not avoiding the overall risk of South Korea's tech sector—they are surgically exiting the memory chip segment, the area with the most concentrated controversy. Concerns about a memory cycle peak have been fully expressed through the extreme polarization of positioning structures.
The Divergence Between Earnings Forecasts and Market Pricing
In stark contrast to the foreign capital exodus, the analyst community continues to raise earnings forecasts. Consensus 2027 EPS estimates for South Korea's tech sector were revised up 8% over the past three months, with cumulative upward revisions reaching 122% over the past six months. While this data covers the broader tech sector rather than a pure memory chip calculation, the directional signal is hard to ignore.
The market is pricing in cyclical peak risk, while sell-side research institutions keep raising their forward earnings outlooks. This divergence itself constitutes the core tension in the current South Korean semiconductor investment thesis.
From a valuation perspective, South Korea's semiconductor sector currently trades at just 4.7x forward earnings, versus a historical average of 10.6x—a significant discount. But low valuation alone does not constitute a margin of safety. The inherent pattern of the memory chip industry is that valuations tend to look cheapest precisely when earnings are near their peak. If this is indeed an earnings peak, the denominator—earnings—could deteriorate rapidly, and 4.7x P/E would no longer represent undervaluation but rather a classic peak-earnings trap.
Can HBM Expansion Extend the Cycle?
The key question is whether we are truly at an earnings peak. The continued expansion of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) demand offers an important counterargument to the cycle-peak thesis.
According to TrendForce data, the firm raised its 2027 HBM price outlook in September and projects HBM will absorb 30% of DRAM wafer input by 2027, up from 22% in 2026. More wafer resources flowing to HBM production means available capacity for traditional DRAM will be squeezed, potentially extending the tight supply environment. The market worries about a memory cycle peak, but HBM's own expansion may be precisely what prolongs the traditional memory cycle.
However, industry forecasts supporting sustained pricing power do not necessarily lock in margin trajectories for Samsung Electronics or SK Hynix. HBM growth does not automatically mean the memory cycle is about to reverse—this logical chain still awaits data validation.
Near-Term Earnings Pressure and Target Price Adjustments
Beyond the macro narrative, near-term earnings signals also warrant attention. DS Investment & Securities released a report on September 29 noting that Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix may report Q3 results below market consensus.
The firm's analyst Lee Soo-rim (phonetic) projects Q3 operating profits for memory chip makers at 10.4 trillion won for Samsung Electronics and 7 trillion won for SK Hynix. These figures fall below current market consensus (11.1 trillion won for Samsung Electronics, 7.8 trillion won for SK Hynix), with sequential growth of only about 16%.
He attributes the earnings shortfall primarily to the Korean won's roughly 11% depreciation against the U.S. dollar from the end of Q2. Additionally, rising costs in Samsung Electronics' Mobile Experience (MX) business, one-time expenses in its visual display and home appliance divisions, and SK Hynix's shipment mix changes and revenue recognition timing adjustments during the transition to next-generation HBM products all weighed on Q3 results.
He emphasizes, however, that the market has already fully priced in currency-driven earnings pressure, and the real focus should be on Q4. As HBM4 revenue contribution expands, earnings improvement is expected to gain new momentum.
2027 HBM Pricing Power as the Core Variable
Lee further notes that 2027 HBM average selling prices could see additional upside. Rising costs for base dies and back-end processes from the transition to 8-high stacking, combined with higher general-purpose DRAM prices, are strengthening HBM's pricing power.
From a technical standpoint, transitioning stacking layers from current levels to 8-high theoretically increases the number of HBM stacks that can be manufactured from the same quantity of DRAM dies by 50%. As graphics processing unit (GPU) shipments expand, the bottleneck previously concentrated on the DRAM die side is shifting toward base dies and back-end processes.
This bottleneck migration has already triggered ripple effects across the supply chain. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing's accelerated CoWoS advanced packaging capacity expansion and increased outsourcing, along with Samsung Electronics' greater allocation of advanced-node capacity for HBM base dies and back-end process investments, are all seen as responses to this structural shift.
Based on these assessments, DS Investment & Securities maintains its ₩530,000 (approximately $390) target price on Samsung Electronics while lowering SK Hynix's target from ₩3.1 million (approximately $2,300) to ₩2.64 million (approximately $1,900), maintaining Buy ratings on both companies.
Re-rating or Trap: The Data Will Decide
The current investment logic for South Korean memory chips is not complicated. If 2027 HBM contract prices remain strong and traditional DRAM supply stays tight, the market will be forced to reprice for a longer earnings cycle. With foreign ownership at extreme lows, such a re-rating, once triggered, could unfold with considerable intensity.
Conversely, if supply rapidly catches up with demand, the 4.7x P/E will reveal its true nature—the classic form of a peak-earnings trap.
The key indicators that will determine the direction are 2027 HBM contract pricing trends, as well as changes in traditional DRAM spot prices and major manufacturers' profit margins. Low valuation itself is not a catalyst—the data is.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan welcomed a joint statement issued Monday by the US, Japan, and South Korea reaffirming the importance of peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait.
Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍) thanked the three countries for the statement. He welcomed the international community’s continued attention to regional security and support for Taiwan’s inclusion in international organizations.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Japanese Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu, and South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York.
The ministers “encouraged the peaceful resolution of cross-Strait issues and opposed any attempts to unilaterally change the status quo,” according to the US State Department.
The statement also expressed support for Taiwan’s meaningful participation in appropriate international organizations. It underscored support for “freedom of navigation and overflight, unimpeded lawful commerce, and other lawful uses of the sea for all nations in the Indo-Pacific and globally,” in accordance with international law as reflected in the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
Taiwan’s foreign ministry said stability in the Taiwan Strait is vital to Indo-Pacific security, the global economy, and supply chains. It added that Taiwan would strengthen its self-defense and societal resilience, safeguard the status quo, and deepen cooperation with the US, Japan, South Korea, and other democratic partners.
The ministry said it would continue working with international partners to secure Taiwan’s meaningful participation in international organizations, enabling the country to contribute more to addressing global challenges.
National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) also welcomed the trilateral statement in a post on X Tuesday. He described the announcement as “a powerful statement against coercive behaviors by the PRC in the Indo-Pacific.”

articles.title: South Korea central bank maintains restraint as economic boom extends - Traders Union
articles.summary: South Korea central bank maintains restraint as economic boom extends  Traders Union
articles.full_text:
South Korea’s economic expansion continues to gather pace as overseas demand for AI-related materials supports the country’s growth outlook. Rising inflation is adding pressure on policymakers, but the Bank of Korea is showing restraint rather than moving aggressively to curb the boom.
Highlights
- Bank of Korea maintains a measured policy approach as rapid economic expansion and accelerating inflation persist under the new chief's leadership.
- The ongoing economic boom is largely supported by external demand, especially for AI-related materials exported by South Korean firms.
- The central bank's restraint aims to allow the boom to naturally plateau while minimizing disruption for industries profiting from global technology demand.
Policy stance amid strong growth
As reported by Bloomberg, the Bank of Korea is keeping a measured policy stance despite the rapid clip of expansion and a pickup in inflation.
The central bank’s new chief is presented as avoiding panic and allowing the current growth spurt to reach a natural ceiling before easing gradually. That approach suggests officials see the present boom as strong, but not yet in need of a forceful policy response.
External demand shapes the outlook
The current expansion is driven not only by domestic conditions but also by overseas demand, particularly for AI-related materials supplied by South Korean companies.
That external engine gives the boom broader support, while also complicating the central bank’s task as it manages spillover effects. For the wider economy, a restrained response could help preserve momentum while limiting disruption to companies benefiting from global technology demand.
Meta’s Meta Enterprise Platform rollout was the focus of our earlier coverage, highlighting the company’s push to package its AI models, agents and tools for business users. We noted that bundling Muse with enterprise-focused agents and coding tools points to a broader monetization strategy for Meta’s AI spending beyond consumer apps, with knock-on implications for AI infrastructure demand across the tech ecosystem.

articles.title: Japan and South Korea must master transactional diplomacy - Engelsberg Ideas
articles.summary: Japan and South Korea must master transactional diplomacy  Engelsberg Ideas
articles.full_text:
The United States is reviewing its military commitments in East Asia. Seoul and Tokyo must learn to compete for Washington's support.
Southwest of Tokyo lies the quaint city of Nara. As the capital of Imperial Japan from AD 710 to 784, Nara gained renown for its historic shrines and roaming deer, the latter of which crave being fed Japanese snacks (senbei) by visitors. Nara Prefecture is also the hometown of Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi.
Self-styled as Japan’s answer to Margaret Thatcher, Takaichi’s premiership has been characterised by one of the most robust increases in defence spending and shifts in security policy since the Second World War, not least the relaxation of decades-old rules governing arms exports. Both Japan and South Korea have realised that their regional and global security environments are worsening. This is not only a result of isolated threats from an ever more aggressive Beijing or a nuclear Pyongyang. Rather, alliances old and new, including growing ties between Russia and North Korea, have been accompanied by heightened collusion between Moscow, Beijing, Pyongyang and Tehran. For Seoul, Tokyo and Washington, the individual and collective threats posed by these alignments of authoritarian actors can no longer be ignored.
The junior partner in any alliance fears two possibilities: the first is entrapment, wherein they can do little but follow their senior partner’s edicts, whether that means being dragged into an unwanted war or otherwise. The second is abandonment, a fear that is increasingly on the minds of policymakers in Tokyo and Seoul. President Trump’s announcement of the scaling-down of the annual US-South Korean Ulchi Freedom Shield military exercises on 16 August, hours before the drills were due to begin, caused unease in Seoul. Whether on grounds of cost, a penchant to revive talks with Kim Jong Un or a combination of the two, this was not the first time Trump had performed such an act. During his first administration, similar drills were downsized and cancelled.
Fears of such abandonment are not new. After the Korean War Armistice Agreement was signed in July 1953, and as South Korea’s army expanded, President Eisenhower called for a drawdown of US forces on the Korean Peninsula. Troop numbers dropped from over 325,000 in 1953 to little more than 75,000 in 1955. Nearly two decades later, the Nixon administration’s Guam Doctrine led to a further reduction in troops to a little over 40,000 by 1971, a retrenchment that catalysed South Korea’s own – albeit abortive – ambitions for nuclear weapons. More recently, under George W. Bush, approximately 3,600 troops were redeployed to Iraq in 2004, never to return to the peninsula.
Yet, the West’s allies must realise that the world of today is nothing like that after the Second World War, in which Washington financed the rebuilding of what was to become East Asia’s security architecture. The signing of mutual defence treaties, notably with Seoul and Tokyo, and the bolstering of alliances have become invaluable in deterring an expanding array of threats. Today’s world, however, shows that not all alliances are the same. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov claimed recently that the ‘invincible alliance’ between North Korea and Russia is fighting to establish a ‘new’ and ‘just’ world order.
Even though Moscow, Pyongyang, Beijing and Tehran use similar rhetoric to that of the US and its allies to describe their relations (such as ‘comprehensive’ and ‘strategic’), what makes these new sets of authoritarian alliances particularly concerning is that not all of them are codified. The members of this deadly quartet have neither signed any treaty nor pledged adherence to a common framework. The specifics of any respective bilateral alliance are also shrouded in secrecy.
Facing these new alignments in global politics, Washington’s longstanding ironclad alliances with Seoul and Tokyo need to be strengthened, but Seoul and Tokyo cannot simply expect their larger ally to do all the work. For all the supposed shared values between Washington’s allies and partners, like-mindedness does not preclude competition for the attention of a common senior ally. Discussions surrounding the redeployment of Patriot missile batteries from South Korea to the Middle East, in March and April this year, underscore this reality.
South Korea’s progressive president Lee Jae Myung has spent his first year in power trying to move away from his pre-election jibes against the US-South Korean alliance. One of his first manoeuvres after having met President Trump in August 2025 was to raise defence spending for 2027 to an all-time high of 73 trillion South Korean won (just over $54 billion), a significant increase of 8.2 per cent from the previous year. This justified move, coupled with Seoul’s commitment to raise defence spending to 3.5 per cent of its GDP by 2035 (current levels amount to approximately 2.3 per cent), is indicative of a realisation that, amid a deteriorating regional and global security environment, Seoul must simultaneously strengthen its relationship with Washington while taking steps to modernise this alliance.
Rhetoric, however, is not synonymous with reality. For Seoul, bolstering its alliance with Washington means following through promptly on prior commitments. Despite having pledged almost a year ago to invest $350 billion in the United States (in response to a reduction in US tariffs on South Korean exports, from 25 to 15 per cent), South Korea’s dithering has understandably irritated the White House. Faced with the threat of possible tariff hikes, following a recent visit to Washington, South Korea’s Trade Minister, Kim Jung-kwan, stressed how negotiations for a $100 billion investment into nuclear power plants and natural-gas projects are now in their final stages.
In contrast, in July 2025, Japan legally committed to investing $550 billion into the US economy until 2029 and has so far launched two energy and manufacturing infrastructure projects totalling $109 million. Japan’s promptness, agreeing to transfer funds within 45 days of the US selecting a particular investment project, reflects a recognition within Tokyo that boosting defence spending and reinforcing the alliance with the United States go hand in hand: the former reinforces the latter.
Yet this difference between Seoul and Tokyo must also be understood with respect to the perennial question of domestic politics. In contrast to his Japanese counterpart, South Korea’s Lee Jae Myung faces constraints from his own party and voter base, for whom strengthening ties with Washington remains contentious.
When I visited Nara earlier this month, the deer were far from shy or deferential. The sight of me holding a pack of senbei drove a small herd to fight over every morsel. The stag scoffed most of them, leaving the rest to fend over the dregs. Like the senbei, the United States is a scarce resource. Washington must commit itself to its East Asian allies: the security of the Korean peninsula is a direct security interest of the United States. Nevertheless, as the West faces an expanding number of threats, Washington’s attention cannot stretch into infinity. Just as the stag did not wait to push past the rest of the herd, Seoul and Tokyo must recognise that allies who hesitate at a moment of opportunity risk being outpaced by a quicker partner. While there is as yet no active US retrenchment from East Asia, ironclad does not mean unconditional. As in any herd, the deer that dithers goes hungry.

articles.full_text:
On September 28, Japanese and South Korean stock markets declined, led by significant losses in South Korea's KOSPI, which fell 2.70%, while Japan's Nikkei 225 dropped 0.73%. Large-cap tech stocks faced heavy pressure, highlighted by sharp drops in Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. Market sentiment was dampened by SK Hynix subsidiary Solidigm's potential U.S. IPO plans, prompting scrutiny of SK Group's ownership structure and weighing on the semiconductor sector. Additionally, geopolitical risks resurfaced in the Middle East after Trump rejected an Iranian proposal, and Tehran maintained its hardline stance on reopening a critical waterway, compounding regional tensions.

Meanwhile, after Trump rejected a proposal from Iran, market concerns over escalating tensions in the Middle East resurfaced. Tehran maintained its stance on a seven-day plan to reopen the critical waterway and stated that it would not ease the related conditions.

articles.title: South Korea's KOSPI Falls Below 7,000 After Chuseok Holiday as Semiconductor Heavyweights Slide - finance.biggo.com
articles.summary: South Korea's KOSPI Falls Below 7,000 After Chuseok Holiday as Semiconductor Heavyweights Slide  finance.biggo.com
articles.full_text:
South Korea's KOSPI surrendered the 7,000 level in early trading as markets reopened after the Chuseok holiday. With upward pressure on U.S. long-term Treasury yields persisting, foreign and institutional investors sold in tandem, and semiconductor heavyweights including Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix dragged the index lower.
According to the Korea Exchange, as of 9:49 a.m. on September 28, the KOSPI was trading at 6,998.62, down 82.30 points (1.16%) from the previous session. The index opened at 7,057.86, down 23.06 points (0.33%), before extending losses to an intraday low of 6,989.34.
By investor category, foreigners net sold 382.5 billion won (approximately $281.8 million) and institutions net sold 21.7 billion won (approximately $16.0 million) on the main KOSPI board. Retail investors absorbed the selling with net purchases of 171 billion won (approximately $126.0 million), but it was not enough to stem the decline.
Market-cap heavyweights Samsung Electronics (005930.KS) and SK Hynix (000660.KS) both traded lower. Samsung Electronics was down 6,000 won (approximately $4.4), or 2.10%, at 279,500 won (approximately $210), while SK Hynix fell 50,000 won (approximately $37), or 2.69%, to 1.812 million won (approximately $1,300).
Samsung Electronics' decline was compounded by supply-demand factors ahead of its ex-dividend date. Today is the last day to buy shares to receive the third-quarter dividend, with September 30 as the record date and September 29 as the ex-dividend date. The market expects Samsung Electronics' third-quarter dividend per share to be around 4,500 won (approximately $3.3).
In contrast, Samsung Electro-Mechanics (1.59%), LG Energy Solution (4.55%), Hyundai Motor (0.99%), and Samsung Biologics (1.46%) all gained. Samsung Electronics preferred shares (-3.98%), SK Square (-5.21%), and KB Financial (-0.06%) declined.
The KOSDAQ moved in the opposite direction from the KOSPI. At the same time, the KOSDAQ index was trading at 860.39, up 15.91 points (1.88%) from the previous session. On the KOSDAQ market, foreigners and institutions net bought 85.5 billion won (approximately $63.0 million) and 1.5 billion won (approximately $1.1 million) respectively, while retail investors net sold 83.6 billion won (approximately $61.6 million). Alteogen (2.80%), EcoPro BM (3.81%), and Jusung Engineering (0.24%) all rose.
The divergent moves between the KOSPI and KOSDAQ can be explained by two factors.
flowchart TD
    A[Rising U.S. long-term yields] --> B[Valuation pressure on tech stocks]
    B --> C[Weakness in semiconductor heavyweights]
    E[Agent AI proliferation] --> F[Increased inference workloads]
    F --> G[Expectations for server expansion and DRAM demand recovery]
    G --> C
    C --> D[KOSPI breaks below 7,000]
U.S. markets during the holiday: rate pressure and AI momentum coexist
While South Korean markets were closed from September 23–25, U.S. equities faced downward pressure from surging Treasury yields but rebounded on the final trading day. Over the three sessions, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 0.1%, the S&P 500 slipped 0.3%, and the Nasdaq Composite declined 0.6%.
The decline was driven by rising U.S. long-term Treasury yields. The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield spiked to 5.2% intraday on September 24, while the 30-year yield topped 5.5%. On September 25, the 10-year yield partially retraced to 5.1604% but remained elevated. Concerns grew that capital flowing into the bond market could pressure equities, particularly technology stocks.
However, on September 25, Microsoft unveiled a super application integrating its enterprise AI service "Copilot," restoring investor sentiment around AI-related names. Microsoft rose 3.66%, and Dell gained 5.0% on expectations of expanding AI data center server demand. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index climbed 1.41%.
The U.S.-China summit agreement to extend the trade war truce by two months through January next year also provided a positive boost to sentiment. However, assessments suggest that meaningful progress on core issues such as rare earths and advanced semiconductors remained limited.
The performance of U.S. markets during the holiday and South Korean markets on September 28 is summarized below.

|---|---|---|
| Dow Jones Industrial Average | Sept 23–25 cumulative | -0.1% | 
| S&P 500 | Sept 23–25 cumulative | -0.3% | 
| Nasdaq | Sept 23–25 cumulative | -0.6% | 
| Philadelphia Semiconductor Index | Sept 25 single day | +1.41% | 
| KOSPI | Sept 28 intraday | -1.16% | 
| KOSDAQ | Sept 28 intraday | +1.88% | 
Attention shifts to major events later this week
The stock market this week is expected to digest U.S. long-term yields, key economic indicators, and Micron's earnings in succession, continuing the battle around the 7,000 level. In particular, the U.S. September nonfarm payrolls report, August personal consumption expenditures (PCE), and South Korea's September export data are cited as key variables that will shape expectations for future rates and corporate earnings.
The direction of semiconductor stocks will likely hinge on Micron's earnings, scheduled for later this week. With the recent proliferation of agent AI such as GPT-6 and Muse fueling expectations for increased inference workloads, server expansion, and improved DRAM demand, the key question is what outlook Micron will provide for next-quarter profitability and memory demand.
Micron is one of the world's three largest DRAM producers, with a production base in Higashihiroshima, Hiroshima Prefecture, Japan. In September 2025, Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) agreed to provide up to 536 billion yen (approximately $3.4 billion) in support for Micron's next-generation DRAM mass production plans at its Hiroshima plant, and Micron plans to invest 1.5 trillion yen (approximately $9.5 billion) in the same facility, targeting first shipments around 2028.
South Korean export data is also a variable. South Korea's exports for September 1–20 surged 78.3% year-over-year, with semiconductor exports soaring 259.4%. With Micron's earnings and South Korea's September export data set to be released sequentially around October 1 (South Korea time), some observers note that semiconductor stock volatility could temporarily increase as these events are digested.
Han Ji-young, an analyst at Kiwoom Securities, expects the KOSPI to battle around the 7,000 level this week, influenced by U.S. Treasury yields, employment data, domestic exports, and Micron's earnings. He presented a weekly expected range of 6,800–7,250.
"The recent releases of GPT-6 and Muse are creating a narrative of 'agent AI market expansion → increased inference workloads → server expansion → improved DRAM demand,'" he said. "Market attention is also likely to focus on comments regarding memory demand and price changes during Micron's conference call."
He added, "Uncertainty surrounding rising U.S. long-term yields will persist, but the recovery in leadership of AI infrastructure stocks, including agent AI-driven semiconductor names, will provide upside momentum for the market. A strategy of treating volatility that emerges while digesting major events clustered later this week—Micron's earnings, exports, and employment data—as an opportunity to increase equity exposure remains valid."

articles.title: US, Japan and South Korea launch economic-security talks despite Xi's summit in Washington - The Star
articles.summary: US, Japan and South Korea launch economic-security talks despite Xi's summit in Washington  The Star
articles.full_text:
The United States, Japan and South Korea announced a new economic-security consultation and reinforced their support for stability across the Taiwan Strait on Monday, sending a coordinated message on two of Beijing’s most sensitive issues just days before Chinese President Xi Jinping’s summit with US President Donald Trump.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Japanese Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu and South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun unveiled the initiative after meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
The three governments pledged to stand against economic coercion and “non-market policies and practices” that produce harmful industrial overcapacity and distort markets, as well as arbitrary export restrictions that disrupt global supply chains.
They also agreed to strengthen an existing trilateral supply-chain early warning system, according to a joint statement released by the US State Department.
Trump is scheduled to meet Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi on Tuesday, two days before his talks with Xi at the White House, giving Tokyo an opportunity to convey its priorities directly to the US president ahead of the summit.
Takaichi also met Trump at the White House in March, less than two months before the US president travelled to Beijing for talks with Xi.
Trump spoke with her again by phone after the May summit, providing what Takaichi described as a detailed account of his discussions with the Chinese leader.
Xi is expected to arrive in the United States on Wednesday for a three-day state visit, with trade, artificial intelligence and other economic and security issues expected to feature prominently in his meeting with Trump.
China not identified as target of new economic-security consultation
The trilateral statement did not identify China as the target of the new economic-security consultation. But its references to economic coercion, industrial overcapacity and export restrictions closely tracked long-standing complaints by Washington and its Asian allies about Beijing’s economic practices.
China’s dominance of critical-mineral processing and its restrictions on exports of some strategically important materials have become major concerns for the US and other advanced economies seeking to reduce their dependence on Chinese supply chains.
The statement also called for closer cooperation among the three countries on semiconductors and for stronger protections around critical and emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence, quantum technology, digital infrastructure and biotechnology.
The three governments said they would “cooperatively reinforce advanced-technology stacks and supply chain resilience” and expressed interest in expanding cooperation among their national laboratories.
The announcement comes as Washington and Beijing hold their own economic talks ahead of the Xi-Trump summit.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer met Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng in New York over the weekend to discuss possible summit deliverables, including trade and artificial intelligence.
Taiwan Strait concerns raised at meeting
Alongside the economic-security measures, Rubio, Motegi and Cho emphasised the importance of maintaining peace and stability across the Taiwan Strait and encouraged the peaceful resolution of cross-strait disputes.
They opposed unilateral attempts to change the status quo and expressed support for Taiwan’s “meaningful participation” in appropriate international organisations.
The language is likely to draw scrutiny from Beijing, which regards Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary.
Most countries, including the United States, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.
The three officials also supported freedom of navigation and overflight, unimpeded lawful commerce and other lawful uses of the sea in the Indo-Pacific, in accordance with international law as reflected in the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea.
On energy security, Washington, Tokyo and Seoul agreed to work towards stronger regional supply resilience by increasing oil stockpiles and encouraging cooperation between energy-producing and consuming countries.
They also committed to implementing a July memorandum to accelerate the deployment of small modular nuclear reactors in third countries under nuclear safety, security and non-proliferation standards.
The meeting also covered North Korea, with the three officials reaffirming their commitment to the complete denuclearisation of the Korean peninsula and calling on Pyongyang to return to dialogue.
They pledged to continue efforts against revenue-generating activities that support North Korea’s nuclear and ballistic missile programmes, including illicit cyber operations and the overseas deployment of North Korean information-technology workers.
Rubio reiterated US defence commitments to Japan and South Korea, including Washington’s extended nuclear deterrence, while the three countries promised to continue security cooperation and consultations at all levels. -- SOUTH CHINA MORNING POST

articles.summary: US export controls on chips were not a key topic at Xi-Trump summit — South China Morning Post  UA.NEWS
articles.full_text:
During the summit between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in Washington, US export controls on chip supplies to China were likely not among the main topics of the talks. The final statements from Beijing and Washington on the meeting’s results contain no direct mention of these restrictions, South China Morning Post reports.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC that export control issues related to national security were not considered as part of this week’s trade negotiations. China’s Foreign Ministry, in announcing eight outcomes of the summit, also did not mention US technology restrictions. Among the agreements, Beijing cited the launch of a China-US dialogue on artificial intelligence risks.
Restrictions remain in force
The absence of public disputes does not mean the restrictions have been lifted. The Trump administration has largely retained rules introduced by Joe Biden’s administration in October 2022 that restrict China’s access to advanced chips and equipment for their production.
At the beginning of Trump’s second term, the United States also banned exports to China of Nvidia’s H20 chip, which the company developed in line with US rules. According to Brookings fellow Kyle Chan, China has likely become more confident about the existing restrictions due to the development of its own advanced semiconductor supply chain.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
Beijing’s bet on domestic production
Paul Triolo, a partner at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, believes Beijing is satisfied with the progress of its semiconductor industry despite US controls. According to a forecast by a Taipei-based research company, the share of Nvidia, AMD and other foreign suppliers will decline to 21% in 2026 from 34% last year.
Previously, Beijing resisted efforts by Trump and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang to return the less powerful H200 chips to the Chinese market. Chinese authorities later allowed a limited number of technology companies to buy these chips in set volumes. Nvidia wrote off $400 million in the first half of the year due to excess H200 inventory caused by approval delays.
Triolo warned that the current pause may be temporary. He drew attention to legislative initiatives in the US Congress, including the Match Act, which is intended to encourage Washington’s allies, including Japan and the Netherlands, to coordinate restrictions on sales of advanced chipmaking equipment to China. According to Triolo, Chinese officials may view new restrictions as a violation of agreements reached in Busan in October 2025 and respond by expanding controls over rare earth metals and equipment for their production.

articles.title: Quandela Establishes South Korea as Asian Hub for Photonic QPU Manufacturing and Hardware R&D - Quantum Computing Report
articles.summary: Quandela Establishes South Korea as Asian Hub for Photonic QPU Manufacturing and Hardware R&D  Quantum Computing Report
articles.full_text:
French photonic quantum computing manufacturer Quandela has unveiled a strategic framework establishing South Korea as its primary Asian hub for quantum processor manufacturing, system integration, and collaborative R&D. Announced in Seoul, the initiative targets semiconductor-level fabrication of integrated photonic QPU modules, component co-development, and hybrid high-performance computing (HPC) software integration, complementing the company’s regional operations across Europe and North America (via its Quandela Federal defense subsidiary).
The manufacturing strategy seeks to form an industrial consortium involving South Korean semiconductor foundries (such as Samsung Electronics and SK hynix) and optoelectronic system integrators (including LG Innotek) to scale mass production of photonic control chips and optical component packaging. Under the proposed intellectual property framework, pre-existing IP remains with individual partners, while co-developed manufacturing protocols and integrated optical modules will be shared based on institutional contributions.

|---|---|---|
| Partner Entity / Institution | Hardware & Research Domain | Technical Scope & Deployment Roadmap | 
| • KAIST (Son Young-ik Research Group) | • Optical component & electronic control co-design | • Integrating Korean-developed electronic control modules directly into Quandela QPU chassis in Paris | 
| • KRIBB (Bio-Research Institute) | • Photonic QPU molecular simulation | • Proof-of-concept quantum molecular modeling for drug discovery and algorithmic validation | 
| • Seoul Metropolitan Govt (₩80B MOU Alignment) | • Regional QPU cluster & supply chain hub | • Expanding local subsidiary (Quandela Korea) from 3 to 10 systems engineers by 2027 |

The initiative integrates with ongoing QPU software optimizations. Collaborating with NVIDIA, Quandela reduced GPU-to-QPU communication latency to the millisecond regime, enabling high-speed hybrid error mitigation and job execution across HPC supercomputing clusters (such as the 12-qubit Lucy processor deployed at France’s TGCC facility). Simultaneously, hardware engineering teams from KAIST are deploying to Paris to integrate Korean-fabricated electronic control units into Quandela’s physical QPU chassis, establishing a cross-border supply chain for full-stack fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC).

articles.full_text:
Excess tax revenue in South Korea could exceed 50 trillion won, or US$36.9 billion, this year. This estimate is linked, in particular, to a stronger-than-expected cycle in the semiconductor industry, Taipei Times reports, citing Yonhap News.
Reserves and strategic investments
According to Yonhap’s calculations, this could increase the Future Response Fund to more than 200 trillion won. This government mechanism directs excess tax revenue toward strategic investments and fiscal reserves.
According to Yonhap, South Korea’s Ministry of Economy and Finance expects to release a revised estimate of national tax revenue for 2026 later this month. At the same time, the ministry said that no final decision on the revised estimate has yet been made.
More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram.
Budget financing
The additional revenue will give the government more room to increase spending without a corresponding increase in borrowing. In the 2027 budget proposal, a significant share of semiconductor-related revenue is planned to be directed toward artificial intelligence, chip manufacturing and youth support, as well as limiting bond issuance and building up a financial reserve.
Economic growth
Last month, the Bank of Korea raised its benchmark interest rate by 0.25 percentage points to 3%. This was the second consecutive increase amid stronger-than-expected economic growth and persistent core inflation. The central bank also raised its GDP growth forecast for this year from 2.6% to 3.3%, citing robust exports and investment spurred by global AI development.
The upswing in the semiconductor cycle supported corporate profits and investment in the country. At the same time, policymakers are assessing how these results will affect household consumption and the broader domestic economy.

articles.title: Chip, Shipbuilding Exports to Stay Strong in Q4, Trade Group Says - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: Chip, Shipbuilding Exports to Stay Strong in Q4, Trade Group Says  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
South Korea's exports of semiconductors, ships and other mainstay products are expected to keep improving in the fourth quarter, after cumulative exports topped $700 billion (about 950 trillion won) earlier this month, surpassing last year's annual total. Rising raw material costs driven by strong energy prices were cited as the biggest variable.
The Export Business Survey Index (EBSI) for the fourth quarter came in at 111.3, up 4.3 points from 107.0 in the previous quarter and above the 100 baseline for a fifth straight quarter, according to a report on fourth-quarter export conditions released on the 26th by the Institute for International Trade at the Korea International Trade Association. The EBSI gauges how Korean exporters view business conditions for the coming quarter. A reading above 100 means exporters expect conditions to improve from the previous quarter.
Seven of 15 product categories were expected to see better export conditions. Semiconductors led with a reading of 140.7, the brightest outlook for a sixth consecutive quarter. Analysts attribute the strength to growing demand for server memory as big tech companies expand artificial intelligence investment, along with chip prices holding at high levels. Ships posted a reading of 138.0, supported by a large order backlog and new orders tied to an expansion of liquefied natural gas (LNG) projects.
By contrast, household goods, at 79.0, and textiles and apparel, at 80.1, were expected to deteriorate on slowing consumption in major markets and intensifying competition from low- and mid-priced products made in China and Southeast Asia. Agricultural and fishery products, at 86.5, were also seen remaining weak as higher oil prices push up refrigeration and freight costs.
Four of 10 subcategories were expected to improve, including export consultations and contracts at 109.5 and capacity utilization at 106.2. Export consultations and contracts stayed above the baseline for a fifth straight quarter on solid export demand. The outlook was most positive for semiconductors, where AI-related demand is expanding, and for wireless communication devices, where new products are expected to lift sales.
Higher raw material prices stemming from strong energy costs were the most frequently cited obstacle to exports, at 20.4%. Greater volatility in the won exchange rate followed at 16.5%, and higher logistics costs tied to renewed geopolitical tensions at 15.2%.
"We expect the improvement in exports to continue in the fourth quarter, led by mainstay items such as semiconductors and ships," said Lee Jun-ho, a researcher at the Korea International Trade Association. "But risk management at the corporate level and policy support are needed so that uncertainty over external variables such as raw material prices, exchange rates and logistics costs does not erode corporate profitability."

articles.title: France’s Quandela taps South Korea as Asian quantum manufacturing hub - DongA Science
articles.summary: France’s Quandela taps South Korea as Asian quantum manufacturing hub  DongA Science
articles.full_text:
French quantum computing company “Quandela” has identified South Korea as a long-term collaboration partner and unveiled a plan to foster the country as an Asian base for quantum computing manufacturing and research.
Quandela CEO Niccolo Somaschi said at a briefing held in Jongno-gu, Seoul, on the 28th, “Korea is not just a sales market but a core partner,” and proposed major cooperation areas including semiconductor-based hardware manufacturing and system integration, convergence of AI and high-performance computing (HPC), and large-scale industrialization of quantum computers.
Somaschi explained, “In Europe we are working with foundries in the region, and we are looking for manufacturing partners in North America and Asia as well,” adding, “Because quantum computing is a technology of high strategic importance, it is crucial for each region to secure its own manufacturing capabilities.”
Quantum computers are a future strategic technology capable of solving types of problems that are impossible for conventional computers. They perform calculations using “qubits,” information-processing units based on quantum phenomena. Depending on their operating mechanism, the physical implementations of qubits vary and can include superconducting electronic circuits, ions, and neutral atoms. 
Founded in 2017, Quandela develops photonic quantum computers that generate, transmit, and process quantum information using photons, the particles of light. In October 2025, it deployed its 12-qubit quantum computer “Lucy” at the French large-scale computing center TGCC and is supporting a hybrid system by linking it with the Joliot-Curie supercomputer.
At this briefing, Quandela presented the direction for forming a quantum manufacturing consortium involving Korean companies and research institutions. Existing intellectual property (IP) will remain with each institution, while newly created IP will be shared according to the roles and contributions of the partners.
Over the next two years, the company plans to identify domestic partners and create concrete collaboration cases. It cited semiconductor manufacturing technologies of Korean companies such as Samsung Electronics and SK hynix, and LG Innotek’s system integration know-how, as examples.
Quandela also introduced specific ongoing collaboration projects with Korea. The company is jointly developing optical components with Professor Son Young-ik’s team at KAIST. Somaschi said, “KAIST researchers will visit Paris within a few weeks to install electronic components developed in Korea into Quandela’s systems and conduct tests.” Quandela also plans to offer educational programs to the KAIST Quantum Graduate School to contribute to workforce development.
In addition, together with the Korea Research Institute of Bioscience and Biotechnology (KRIBB), Quandela is conducting proof-of-concept molecular simulations using quantum computing for application in new drug development and is currently preparing to publish the research results. The company is also reviewing participation in related government-led projects such as the quantum manufacturing challenge.
Quandela is also continuing follow-up discussions on an approximately 80 billion won (about 800 billion won in Korean notation) business agreement signed with the Seoul Metropolitan Government in November last year. Kim Yoo-seok, head of Quandela Korea, Quandela’s Korean subsidiary, said, “Initially we focused on application fields, but as Seoul has recently been selected as a quantum computing cluster, we are now fleshing out cooperation that also covers manufacturing and systems.”
Other domestic partners highlighted include the Korea Research Institute of Standards and Science (KRISS), Seoul National University, and Yonsei University. Quandela Korea, which currently has three employees, plans to expand its workforce to around ten by next year.
A key technical challenge for today’s quantum computers is correcting the errors that inevitably occur during computation to ensure reliability. Quandela has unveiled a mid- to long-term technology roadmap for fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC), in which the system size and computational performance are scaled up step by step to perform complex calculations over long periods.
Somaschi said, “Through recent collaboration with NVIDIA in the United States, we have reduced the communication time between the graphics processing unit (GPU) and the quantum processing unit (QPU) from tens of seconds to the millisecond (ms) range.” The company plans to realize FTQC by building a hybrid computing environment that integrates HPC infrastructure with quantum computing.
Somaschi added, “Ultimately, scaling the performance of photonic quantum computers depends on semiconductor-level precision in manufacturing and inspection,” and stated, “We will identify Korean partners, assess the mass-production feasibility of photonic modules, and reflect the results in our technology roadmap toward FTQC.”
