French photonic quantum computing company Quandela plans to identify strategic partners in South Korea over the next two years for technology cooperation and joint development spanning quantum chip manufacturing, system integration, demonstration and real-world operation.
Niccolo Somaschi, chief executive of Quandela, announced the Korea business strategy and a medium- to long-term technology roadmap for fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) at a press conference held at Centropolis in Seoul's Jongno district on the 28th.
Quandela builds quantum computing systems that use photons, the particles of light. The company has recently worked with Nvidia to link quantum processing units (QPUs) with graphics processing units (GPUs), pursuing a hybrid combination of quantum computers and existing computing infrastructure. Because semiconductor-grade precision manufacturing and inspection capabilities are essential to mass-produce photonic quantum computers and scale their performance over the long term, the company intends to deepen technology cooperation with Korea and its manufacturing base.
"Combining Quandela's quantum computing expertise with Korea's semiconductor manufacturing technology would make a perfect match," Somaschi said. "Over the next two years, we will identify partners in Korea, review whether photonic modules are suitable for mass production, and reflect the results in our technology roadmap toward FTQC."
Quandela will pursue cooperation with Korean companies and research institutions across three broad areas: quantum hardware, or quantum chip, manufacturing; cryogenic control and system integration; and the quantum operating stack. In manufacturing, it will jointly develop mass-producible photonic modules using Korean semiconductor and photonic technology. The company plans to verify mass-production feasibility using advanced packaging, wafer-level inspection and precision optical alignment technology, and to draw up a joint manufacturing roadmap.
In system integration, the cryogenic environment and high-speed control devices required for quantum computers will be built into a single system. The aim is to create a control system that reduces latency in computation and an integrated environment in which it can be tested. In operations, Quandela will jointly develop error correction technology and technology that links quantum computers to existing computing infrastructure such as GPUs for artificial intelligence, high-performance computing (HPC) and cloud services. On that basis, it will also pursue a proof of concept (PoC) in Korea linking QPUs with HPC.
The company is also considering forming a quantum manufacturing consortium involving Korean companies and research institutions. Under the arrangement, Quandela would provide its own technology and system roadmap along with its experience building and operating QPUs in Europe, while Korean partners would contribute capabilities in semiconductors, photonics, advanced manufacturing and system integration. Existing intellectual property would remain with each institution, while newly developed IP would be shared according to each party's role and contribution. Cooperation with Korea's three main quantum clusters — Seoul, the Jeonnam-Gwangju region, and the southeastern region — was also raised as a possibility. "We see room for cooperation centered on quantum computing in Seoul, quantum communications in Jeonnam-Gwangju, and quantum sensing in Busan, Ulsan and South Gyeongsang Province," Somaschi said.
Samsung, SK hynix (000660) and LG Innotek (011070) were named as potential corporate partners. "There is potential for cooperation with each company in semiconductor manufacturing capabilities and module integration," he said. "We will build tangible cases of cooperation with Korean companies and research institutions, and over the long term develop Korea into a key hub for cooperation across Asia."

articles.title: ‘U.S. trade policy is damaging the U.S. auto industry’: Canada’s purchase of American cars hits new low as Trump’s tariffs backfire on U.S. automakers - Fortune
articles.summary: ‘U.S. trade policy is damaging the U.S. auto industry’: Canada’s purchase of American cars hits new low as Trump’s tariffs backfire on U.S. automakers  Fortune
articles.full_text:
A decade ago, nearly half of new cars hitting Canadian roads were built in America, but after months of restrictive U.S. tariffs, the number of Big Three autos purchased from America’s northern neighbor have dropped precipitously.
Only 28.4% of new-vehicle sales in Canada in the first half of 2026 were U.S.-built, down from 35.4% in the first half of 2025, according to JD Power Canada data. From about 2021 to 2025, the U.S. market share of new vehicles in Canada was roughly 40%.
Auto analysts blame the steep decline on a series of import taxes placed on Canada over the past year and a half, which included a 25% tariff on Canadian-made cars, a levy expected to double and apply to Canadian auto parts, steel, and vehicles on Jan. 1, 2027. Canada imposed countermeasures, including retaliatory tariffs on American-made autos, as well as on steel and aluminum.
The U.S. auto industry relies heavily on Canada, which is the largest export market for American automakers—larger than the next 10 markets combined, according to a Royal Bank of Canada (RBC) analysis published last month. Auto trade between the two countries has topped $100 billion this year, and despite the speed bumps in trade policy, Canada remains America’s largest auto market.
Yet recent trade policies are not only eroding this relationship, analysts warn, but increasing the likelihood the import taxes meant to punish Canada are actually having a larger adverse impact on American automakers.
“The data is irrefutable,” Brian Kingston, CEO of the Canadian Vehicle Manufacturers’ Association, which represents America’s major automakers in Canada, told Automotive News Canada. “By virtually every metric—be it jobs, production, prices, tariff costs—every metric points to the same thing: U.S. trade policy is damaging the U.S. auto industry.”
How tariffs have roiled the U.S. auto industry
At the foundation of the auto industry’s tariff woes is the fact that no vehicle is built in just one country, as they require thousands of components, which are combined in various facilities all around the world. That means U.S. auto companies are still reliant on products from other countries, even for American cars.
While companies like GM and Stellantis reported billions of dollars in losses from tariffs, those increased costs are hitting consumers. Kelley Blue Book estimated tariffs would increase car prices by up to $6,000, which subsequently increases auto taxes, financing, and insurance costs.
When President Donald Trump implemented the first auto tariffs in April 2025, economists also feared the trade restrictions would actually lead to fewer vehicles being produced in the U.S., as a result of so many “American-made” cars actually being assembled in Canada or Mexico before they are finished in the U.S. With fewer cars produced, demand for workers would decrease, a consequence that may already be coming to fruition: There are about 75,000 fewer manufacturing jobs in the U.S. since January 2025, including 25,900 fewer in motor vehicles and parts production. To be sure, reshoring plans, such as Toyota’s announced $3.6 billion San Antonio assembly plant expansion and Ford’s plans to move some production of Lincoln models from China to the U.S. in 2030, could restore some manufacturing roles in the long term.
To make matters worse for U.S. automakers, their shrinking market share in Canada has provided inroads for competitors in Asia and Europe, where it is cheaper to build cars because of more integrated supply chains—and tariffs are actually lower, Kingston told Fortune. For example, Canada’s imports from Japan have increased from 13.7% in the first six months of 2025 to 16.6% in the same period this year, per JD Power data. South Korean imports jumped a percentage point to 15.6% over the same period, while European imports plateaued.
“We’re in this odd situation where it is now more cost-effective to build a car in Japan or Germany, South Korea, Mexico, and bring it into North America than to build here in North America because of all of the mounting tariff costs,” Kingston said. “That does not bode well for the future of North America’s automotive industry.”
The future of U.S.-Canadian trade
Continued strain on U.S.-Canadian relationships could have lasting consequences for years to come. For decades, the U.S. and Canada have shared a close trade relationship in the automotive industry, signing a pact in 1965 that eliminated some import taxes and promised to consolidate the industry across borders. Those ties were strengthened with the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA), and fortified still with the 2020 United States–Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).
However, Trump has declined to renew the USMCA, despite signing the legislation upon the agreement’s creation six years ago. The agreement blunted some tariff impacts by providing carve-outs for auto parts, and its lapse would result in additional supply-chain uncertainty. The Tax Foundation estimated removing USMCA exemptions would increase taxes by $466 billion over the next decade, about $300 per U.S. household next year, and decrease U.S. output by about 0.1%, equating to lost working hours from 95,000 full-time jobs.
The loss of trade diplomacy between the U.S. and Canada won’t just have short-term economic impacts, Kingston argued. It could jeopardize a 60-year-old friendship that buoyed industrial synergy.
“You shrink your market when you take protectionist policies, and you make your industries less competitive,” Kingston said. “This isn’t a winning formula for success, and the longer these tariffs are being in place, the more damage it’s done.”

articles.title: Semiconductor Manufacturing Equipment Market Forecast to 2035: Advanced-Node Logic Demand Drives Growth - IndexBox
articles.summary: Semiconductor Manufacturing Equipment Market Forecast to 2035: Advanced-Node Logic Demand Drives Growth  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Applied Materials
Broadest product portfolio
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Semiconductor Manufacturing Equipment market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global semiconductor manufacturing equipment market is entering a structurally different growth phase as capital expenditure shifts from cyclical capacity additions toward multi-year technology inflections. The transition to gate-all-around transistors, backside power delivery, and High-NA extreme ultraviolet lithography is reshaping demand architecture, qualification pathways, and competitive positioning. Advanced-node logic and foundry capex now anchors the market, while a parallel investment cycle in mature and specialty nodes supports automotive, industrial, and IoT applications.
Procurement models are evolving from transactional equipment purchases toward solution-as-a-service contracts that guarantee uptime, mean-time-between-failures, and process window control, transferring performance risk to equipment OEMs. Geographic concentration of both demand and manufacturing capability remains a defining feature, with Asia-Pacific accounting for the largest share of consumption and equipment spending. Supply chain and geopolitical risks are prompting regional diversification, though technical and qualification barriers make this a gradual process.
Pricing power has shifted upstream to subsystem and component specialists whose intellectual property in precision optics, motion control, and plasma sources is critical for system performance. This report provides a structured, commercially grounded analysis of the market from 2026 to 2035, covering demand drivers, restraints, end-use sectors, regional dynamics, and competitive structure.
The baseline scenario for the semiconductor manufacturing equipment market through 2035 assumes continued expansion, supported by advanced-node logic and foundry capex as gate-all-around transistors and High-NA EUV lithography move into volume production. Demand is expected to be less cyclical than in prior decades because investment is increasingly tied to specific technology transitions rather than blanket capacity builds. The market is forecast to grow at a compound annual growth rate of 6.8% from 2026 to 2035, with the market index reaching 193 by 2035 (2025 = 100).
Advanced-node logic fabrication remains the largest end-use application, while memory, packaging, and test equipment segments also contribute to growth. The baseline assumes no severe global recession, continued government support for semiconductor manufacturing, and gradual resolution of supply chain bottlenecks. Risks to the outlook include export controls, geopolitical tensions, and potential oversupply in mature nodes. However, the structural drivers of AI, electrification, and digitalization are expected to sustain demand for leading-edge and specialty equipment throughout the forecast period.
Advanced node logic fabrication is the largest and most technologically demanding end-use sector for semiconductor manufacturing equipment. Foundries and IDMs are investing heavily in gate-all-around transistor architectures, backside power delivery, and High-NA EUV lithography to produce chips at 3nm and below. These transitions require new deposition, etch, lithography, and metrology tools, driving multi-year capex commitments. Demand-side indicators include leading foundry capex guidance, AI accelerator production volumes, and smartphone processor node migration. Through 2035, the sector will remain the primary growth engine as AI and high-performance computing applications require ever more advanced logic.
Equipment qualification cycles are lengthening, favoring incumbent suppliers with proven process integration capabilities. The shift to solution-as-a-service contracts further embeds equipment vendors in customer operations, creating recurring revenue streams and higher switching costs. Current trend: Growing.
Major trends: Gate-all-around transistor adoption at 3nm and below, High-NA EUV lithography insertion for sub-2nm nodes, Backside power delivery integration, Rising share of AI and HPC chips in leading-edge capacity, and Longer qualification cycles locking in approved vendors.
Representative participants: TSMC, Samsung Electronics, Intel, GlobalFoundries, ASML Holding, and Applied Materials.
Memory fabrication, encompassing DRAM and NAND flash, is a critical end-use sector for semiconductor manufacturing equipment. After a period of oversupply and capex cuts, the sector is recovering as demand for AI servers, high-bandwidth memory, and enterprise storage accelerates. Equipment demand is driven by transitions to advanced DRAM nodes (1-alpha, 1-beta) and 3D NAND with higher layer counts, requiring new etch, deposition, and inspection tools. Demand-side indicators include memory bit growth, HBM capacity announcements, and data center capex. Through 2035, memory fabrication will remain cyclical but with a rising floor due to AI-driven demand.
Equipment vendors with strong positions in memory-specific processes, such as high-aspect-ratio etch and atomic layer deposition, will benefit. The sector also sees growing investment in advanced packaging for HBM integration, creating additional equipment opportunities. Current trend: Cyclical recovery.
Major trends: High-bandwidth memory capacity expansion for AI accelerators, Transition to 1-beta and 1-gamma DRAM nodes, 3D NAND scaling beyond 200 layers, Advanced packaging for memory-logic integration, and Cyclical capex recovery after 2023-2024 downturn.
Representative participants: Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, Micron Technology, Lam Research, Tokyo Electron, and KLA Corporation.
Mature node and specialty fabrication covers processes at 28nm and above, serving automotive, industrial, IoT, and consumer applications. This sector is experiencing sustained demand as chip content per vehicle rises, industrial automation expands, and IoT devices proliferate. Equipment demand includes new tools for capacity expansion, refurbished equipment, and upgrades for specialty processes such as BCD, eNVM, and power discretes. Demand-side indicators include automotive semiconductor content growth, industrial capex, and government incentives for regional fab construction. Through 2035, mature node investment will remain robust, though subject to periodic oversupply concerns.
Equipment vendors with strong presence in 200mm and 300mm mature node tools, as well as those offering refurbishment and service, will find opportunities. The sector is also seeing increased adoption of automation and advanced process control, driving demand for metrology and inspection equipment. Current trend: Steady growth.
Major trends: Automotive semiconductor content growth per vehicle, Government incentives for regional mature node fabs, Rising demand for power discretes and analog ICs, Refurbished equipment market expansion, and Adoption of advanced process control in mature fabs.
Representative participants: Texas Instruments, Infineon Technologies, STMicroelectronics, NXP Semiconductors, Applied Materials, and Screen Holdings.
Advanced packaging and assembly equipment is a fast-growing end-use sector driven by the need for heterogeneous integration, chiplet architectures, and high-bandwidth memory. As Moore's Law slows, advanced packaging becomes critical for performance scaling, requiring equipment for wafer-level packaging, through-silicon vias, microbump formation, and hybrid bonding. Demand-side indicators include AI accelerator packaging complexity, chiplet adoption rates, and HBM integration volumes. Through 2035, this sector will outpace overall equipment market growth as packaging becomes a primary differentiator for leading-edge products. Equipment vendors with expertise in bumping, bonding, and inspection will benefit.
The sector also sees growing investment from foundries and OSATs expanding advanced packaging capacity, creating opportunities for both front-end and back-end equipment suppliers. Current trend: Accelerating.
Major trends: Hybrid bonding for 3D chip stacking, Chiplet and heterogeneous integration adoption, Through-silicon via scaling for HBM, Fan-out wafer-level packaging growth, and Foundry and OSAT capacity expansion in advanced packaging.
Representative participants: TSMC, ASE Technology, Amkor Technology, Besi, ASM Pacific Technology, and Applied Materials.
Test and metrology equipment ensures yield, reliability, and performance across semiconductor manufacturing. This sector includes wafer inspection, defect review, metrology, and final test equipment. Demand is driven by increasing process complexity at advanced nodes, where defect densities must be controlled at near-atomic levels, and by the need for known-good-die testing in advanced packaging. Demand-side indicators include wafer starts, test intensity per chip, and advanced packaging volumes. Through 2035, test and metrology will grow in line with overall equipment demand, with faster growth in advanced nodes and packaging. Equipment vendors with strong positions in optical inspection, e-beam metrology, and RF test will benefit.
The sector also sees growing adoption of AI-based defect classification and predictive analytics, creating software and service opportunities. Current trend: Growing.

articles.summary: Chip Exports and Capex Lift Korea Growth Outlook to 3.7%  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
Major institutions at home and abroad, including the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, are raising their 2026 growth forecasts for South Korea above 3% because semiconductor exports, chip output and facility investment are lifting the economy more than expected. As the global artificial intelligence industry expands, chip exports have surged and investment by related companies has widened, pushing up expectations for an economy that had been projected to stay sluggish.
Forecasts from major institutions have jumped sharply in just a few months. The OECD raised its projection the most. On the 23rd, the organization put South Korea's 2026 growth rate at 3.7%, up 1.1 percentage points from the 2.6% it forecast in June and the largest upward revision among the Group of 20 economies. It also lifted its 2027 forecast to 2.6% from 1.9%, an increase of 0.7 percentage point. Compared with the 1.7% it projected in March, the outlook has been raised by 2 percentage points in six months. The OECD said strong export and output growth would drive this year's expansion, while next year exports would continue to lead growth with support from a gradual recovery in consumption.
The OECD said the spread of AI is supporting investment, output and trade not only in South Korea but worldwide, and raised its global growth forecast for this year to 2.9%, up 0.1 percentage point. It judged that economies are showing considerable resilience to external shocks such as the war in the Middle East as AI-related investment continues. It lowered its forecast for next year to 3.0%, down 0.1 percentage point.
The Asian Development Bank also raised its 2026 growth forecast for South Korea on the same day, to 3.2% from 2.6%. The ADB cited firm recent manufacturing indicators and rising demand for AI chips that is feeding through to export growth. It also pointed to expansionary fiscal policy and a gradual recovery in private consumption on the back of improved corporate earnings. The bank lifted its forecast for next year to 2.3% from 2.0%.
The Korea Development Institute last month raised its 2026 forecast to 3.2% from 2.5%, an increase of 0.7 percentage point. The Bank of Korea also lifted its projection for this year to 3.3% from 2.6% last month, and raised its forecast for next year to 2.9% from 2.1%, reflecting a judgment that the semiconductor cycle will run into next year.
Higher growth, however, is not translating directly into an improvement in conditions that households feel, because inflation is weighing on them. The OECD raised its forecast for South Korea's consumer price inflation this year to 3.0% from 2.6%, an increase of 0.4 percentage point, and lifted its forecast for next year to 2.7% from 2.2%, up 0.5 percentage point. It said the sharply higher growth outlook and a higher projection for international energy prices than at the time of the June forecast would drive prices up. Even so, South Korea's projected inflation for both years remains below the G20 averages of 4.1% and 3.6%.
The ADB the same day kept its inflation forecast for this year unchanged at 2.7%. It said upward price pressure from rising international energy prices and strong domestic demand would persist, but that government price stabilization measures would offset part of it. Next year, it expects inflation to hold at about 2.2% as energy price pressure eases and the effects of tighter monetary policy come through.
External variables still hang over the strong growth outlook. The OECD said international energy prices would gradually stabilize from the fourth quarter of this year, but flagged as key downside risks the possibility that energy prices keep climbing, that supply shocks arise from adverse weather such as El Nino, and that long-term government bond yields rise further. An early end to the war in the Middle East was presented as an upside factor. The OECD said the spread of AI could lift investment and output further, but that concerns about the profitability of related companies and their heavy reliance on leverage bear watching.

articles.title: OECD sharply raises South Korea growth forecast to 3.7% — largest upgrade among G20 - finance.biggo.com
articles.summary: OECD sharply raises South Korea growth forecast to 3.7% — largest upgrade among G20  finance.biggo.com
articles.full_text:
The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) has projected South Korea's economic growth rate at 3.7% for this year. The figure represents a 1.1 percentage-point upgrade from the 2.6% forecast issued in June — the largest upward revision among the Group of 20 (G20) major economies. Robust semiconductor exports driven by the proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) served as the key factor lifting the growth outlook.
According to South Korea's Ministry of Economy and Finance on September 23, the OECD projected South Korea's real gross domestic product (GDP) growth at 3.7% this year in its interim economic outlook released that day. This marks the second consecutive upward revision, following an increase from 1.7% in March to 2.6% in June. The OECD also raised its 2027 growth forecast for South Korea by 0.7 percentage points, from 1.9% to 2.6%.
The magnitude of the adjustment was the largest across all G20 countries. The OECD noted that South Korea was the only country whose growth forecast was raised by more than 1 percentage point. India posted the second-largest upgrade at 0.8 percentage points. Japan and the United States each saw increases of 0.2 percentage points, bringing their forecasts to 0.8% and 2.2%, respectively. If these projections materialize, South Korea's economic growth rate would surpass that of the United States for the first time in four years, since 2022.
A Ministry of Economy and Finance official explained, "Raising a growth forecast by more than 1 percentage point at once is highly unusual unless it reflects a V-shaped rebound following an economic crisis. It signals that corporate exports, investment, and production activity are strong enough to exceed macroeconomic experts' expectations." The official added, "The 3.8% growth recorded in the first half served as the foundation, and the OECD judged that this momentum will continue into the second half."
The OECD projected that South Korea's growth this year will be led by strong exports and rising production, with consumption recovering moderately next year. It also assessed that AI proliferation is underpinning global investment, production, and trade.
With growth far exceeding expectations, inflation forecasts were also revised upward. The OECD raised its consumer price inflation forecast for South Korea this year from 2.6% to 3.0%. The 2027 inflation forecast was also lifted from 2.2% to 2.7%. However, these figures remain below the G20 average inflation rate of 4.1% this year and 3.6% next year.
Global economic growth was projected at 2.9% this year and 3.0% next year. The OECD assessed that the global economy is maintaining resilience despite external shocks, with strong spending on AI-based infrastructure serving as a key pillar of this year's economy. However, it cited persistent energy price increases and supply shocks from adverse weather conditions such as El Niño as major downside risks.
International organizations and credit rating agencies successively raise forecasts to 3% range
On the same day, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) also raised its growth forecast for South Korea this year from 2.6% to 3.2%. This follows consecutive upgrades from 1.9% in April to 2.6% in July. The ADB said the revision reflects export growth driven by expanding global demand for AI semiconductors, expansionary fiscal policy, and a moderate recovery in private consumption supported by solid corporate earnings. Its 2027 forecast was also raised from 2.0% to 2.3%.
Global credit rating agency Fitch Ratings likewise raised its growth forecast for South Korea this year from 2.6% to 3.5% on the same day. Fitch cited the IT and semiconductor upcycle as a growth driver, estimating that net exports will contribute 1.7 percentage points to growth this year. Global semiconductor sales surged 135% year-over-year in July on a U.S. dollar basis, while South Korea's semiconductor exports rose approximately 70% year-over-year during the January–August period.
The growth forecasts from major domestic and international institutions are summarized as follows:
| Institution | 2026 Growth Forecast | Announcement | 
|---|---|---|
| OECD | 3.7% | September | 
| Fitch | 3.5% | September | 
| Bank of Korea | 3.3% | August | 
| ADB | 3.2% | September | 
| KDI | 3.2% | August | 
| Government | 3.0% | July | 
Following last month's upward revisions by the Bank of Korea (3.3%) and the Korea Development Institute (3.2%), the ADB and Fitch joined the 3% range on the same day, further cementing the consensus for high growth in the South Korean economy.
Growth gap with Taiwan — differences in AI spillover channels
A notable aspect of the ADB's latest outlook is the growth gap between South Korea and Taiwan. The ADB projected Taiwan's growth rate this year at 11.0%, far exceeding South Korea's 3.2%. This is effectively in line with the 11.05% forecast issued last month by Taiwan's statistics agency, the Directorate-General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics. If realized, Taiwan would record its highest annual growth rate since 1988 and its first-ever double-digit growth.
For both economies, the core basis for the upgrades is expanding AI semiconductor exports. However, the spillover channels differ. South Korea's growth is driven by semiconductor exports and facility investment, whereas Taiwan's export boom, fueled by AI demand, is spreading to private investment and consumption, amplifying the growth trajectory.
In its August outlook, the KDI analyzed that South Korea's semiconductor boom is clearly evident in exports and facility investment, but the spillover to private consumption remains modest because income gains are concentrated in the semiconductor sector. This contrasts with Taiwanese authorities' references to simultaneous strength across exports, investment, and consumption.
Risk factors also overlap. The ADB cited heightened geopolitical tensions, increased global financial market volatility, and potential export and investment contraction from additional U.S. tariff hikes as major downside risks for South Korea. Taiwanese authorities similarly pointed to Middle East developments, energy prices, U.S. tariff policy, and the sustainability of global corporate AI investment as variables. The durability of the AI investment cycle is effectively a common variable hanging over both economies.
The growth rate for the advanced Asia-Pacific group, which includes South Korea and Taiwan, was raised by 0.5 percentage points from the July forecast to 3.1% this year. Singapore (3.2% → 5.0%) and Hong Kong (3.0% → 4.2%) also saw significant upgrades. Countries positioned along the semiconductor and AI supply chain led this round of upward revisions.
Fitch identified a reduction in AI capital expenditure and stock market correction risk as key risk factors for the South Korean economy. The agency noted that if a scenario involving a 35% plunge in U.S. equities and an investment shock were to materialize, South Korea's economy — with its high concentration in IT and semiconductor industries — would be difficult to insulate from the impact. On the monetary policy front, Fitch expects the Bank of Korea to raise its benchmark rate once more this year to 3.25%, then hold it steady through 2027–2028.

North Korea appears to have tested a hypersonic weapon that could evade missile defences and prove hard to track and intercept, analysts told AFP Wednesday.

South Korea and Japan said Pyongyang fired two short-range ballistic missiles off its east coast Sunday, condemning the launches as threats to regional peace and security.
North Korea did not identify the weapon, saying only that its missile bureau had "successfully tested a new type of weapon" in a demonstration of "ultra-modern defence technology".
Analysts said the weapon appeared to be an upgraded version of North Korea's Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 hypersonic short-range ballistic missile.
With a range of 450 to 600 kilometres (around 280-370 miles), the hypersonic missile is "designed to strike key military facilities across the Korean peninsula within an extremely short period of time", Yang Moo-jin, former president of the University of North Korean Studies in Seoul, told AFP.
Images released by Pyongyang's state media showed leader Kim Jong Un and his daughter Ju Ae watching a screen displaying what appeared to be the missile's flight path, labelled "Hwasongpho-11Ma-1 flight trajectory".
The North Korean leader warned this week that the weapon's advances would give adversaries "an incurable headache and a very cruel and unavoidable blow", according to the official Korean Central News Agency.
Despite long-running UN sanctions, North Korea has enshrined its status as a nuclear-armed state in law, with its leaders repeatedly declaring its atomic arsenal permanent and irreversible.
North Korea has also secured critical backing from Russia alongside its traditional ally China, leaving fewer incentives for it to engage in renewed diplomacy with Washington.
"North Korea may be talking up its own capabilities, but it has clearly reached the point where it can launch weapons of this calibre," Ahn Chan-il, a researcher originally from North Korea, told AFP.
"I believe these tests are less about upgrading its own military capabilities than testing weapons produced by its defence industry to meet Russia's wartime demand."
Since Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine in 2022, North Korea has become a key ally of the Kremlin, sending troops to support Moscow's war effort in return for economic benefits and military technology, analysts say.
Hong Sung-pyo, senior researcher at the Seoul-based Korea Institute for Military Affairs, said that if used against South Korea, the hypersonic weapon would pose a serious threat.
"But a single successful test is not enough to prove its capabilities. If deployed operationally, however, it would be extremely difficult to defend against," he told AFP.
"Because it manoeuvres as it descends during the terminal phase of flight, it is harder to track and intercept than a conventional ballistic missile -- particularly at hypersonic speeds."

Chinese Semiconductor Advances Defy U.S. Export Restrictions
Next-Generation Computing Architectures Reshape the Technology Paradigm
Expanded Patent Offensive and Tighter Research Controls Reinforce Technological Leadership Strategy
China is accelerating the development of a self-sufficient ecosystem spanning memory semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI) chips, and next-generation computing technologies. Despite U.S. export restrictions on advanced semiconductor equipment, the country is advancing its DRAM and NAND technologies while simultaneously stepping up development of next-generation chips and large-scale patent acquisition through universities and research institutes. At the same time, Beijing is expanding research and development (R&D) investment and strengthening control over critical technologies, further enhancing its position in the global race for future semiconductor leadership.
China Expands Semiconductor Ecosystem to Narrow Technology Gap
According to the South China Morning Post (SCMP) on July 6, construction recently began under strict secrecy on a state-of-the-art R&D production line at ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) in Hefei, Anhui Province, widely regarded as the heart of China's semiconductor industry. The project is designed to develop and manufacture next-generation "bonded DRAM," a technology capable of dramatically improving both memory performance and capacity and widely viewed as a potential "game changer" for the memory semiconductor industry. China is also aggressively moving into Compute Express Link (CXL) DRAM, often described as the post-HBM generation of memory technology. Building on its experience mass-producing server-grade DDR5 memory, CXMT has formally announced its entry into the CXL 3.0 market. The company is also deepening cooperation with domestic fabless chip designer Montage Technology and other partners to secure controller technology, one of the most critical components of the ecosystem.
Only two years ago, Chinese memory makers including DRAM specialist CXMT and NAND flash producer Yangtze Memory Technologies Co. (YMTC) were largely confined to manufacturing low-end chips while recording annual losses amounting to billions of dollars. At the time, China's share of the global DRAM market was too small even to be officially measured. By the first quarter of this year, however, CXMT's global DRAM market share had surged to 8%, reflecting tangible results from Beijing's drive for semiconductor self-sufficiency. The company has advanced to the point where it is now being mentioned as a potential new DRAM supplier for Apple, a company well known for imposing exceptionally stringent supplier qualification standards.
What has drawn particular attention is that China has begun staking out leadership in next-generation technologies despite sweeping U.S. restrictions. Although Beijing faced major obstacles after U.S. sanctions effectively blocked imports of ASML's advanced extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography systems—equipment considered indispensable for leading-edge semiconductor manufacturing—it has rapidly developed alternative approaches. CXMT is now reportedly on the verge of launching its own HBM products by employing every available technique, including sophisticated multi-patterning processes that maximize the capabilities of legacy manufacturing nodes. The company has also converted roughly 20% of its production capacity to dedicated HBM manufacturing while making development of HBM3 and HBM3E a strategic priority.
Nor is the conventional DRAM market immune from China's advance. Chinese suppliers are mounting an increasingly visible challenge in the DDR5 segment, now the mainstream memory standard for modern servers and PCs. Ongoing global memory shortages fueled by the semiconductor supercycle have further increased demand for Chinese-made products. Warning signs have already emerged in the NAND flash market. Samsung Electronics and SK hynix currently dominate the high-value segment—including enterprise solid-state drives (eSSDs)—with NAND products in the upper-200-layer to 300-layer range. However, as the industry moves toward ultra-high-layer NAND exceeding 400 layers, manufacturers are encountering fundamental physical limitations, making wafer-to-wafer (W2W) hybrid bonding an essential production technology.
This advanced back-end packaging process directly bonds two semiconductor wafers without conductive bumps, vertically connecting circuitry to achieve significantly higher performance. YMTC currently holds the industry's strongest patent position in this field. The company became the first in the world to commercialize its proprietary Xtacking technology, successfully mass-producing NAND products from 160 layers through its latest 270-layer offerings. YMTC holds 119 core patents related to the technology, significantly outpacing South Korean competitors, including Samsung Electronics with 83 patents and SK hynix with 11 patents as of 2023. Such is YMTC's technological advantage that Samsung, the global NAND market leader, reportedly entered into a patent licensing agreement with the Chinese company to facilitate development of next-generation V10 NAND exceeding 430 layers using a triple-stack architecture.
Having strengthened its competitiveness in memory technologies, China is now accelerating efforts to establish new AI chip design methodologies and system architectures. Huawei's "Tau Law," unveiled in May, is widely viewed as having the potential to reshape the competitive landscape of AI semiconductors. Rather than focusing on chip miniaturization—the primary strategy pursued by South Korean and U.S. companies—the technology takes an entirely different approach by reducing data movement latency to enhance overall system performance.
Peking University and Chinese Academy of Sciences Develop Brain-Inspired Next-Generation Chip
China is also delivering meaningful breakthroughs in next-generation semiconductors. According to The Wall Street Journal, a joint research team led by Professor Yang Yuchao of Peking University's School of Integrated Circuits and researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) recently published in Science, one of the world's most prestigious academic journals, what they described as the world's first integrated artificial neural network-based 40nm Computing-in-Memory (CIM) semiconductor device. The chip overcomes the physical limitations of conventional computer architectures while demonstrating a framework capable of reconstructing the highly complex surface structure of the human brain in less than 0.5 seconds. In terms of computational performance, it reportedly delivers processing efficiency ranging from 50 times to as much as 478 times that of Nvidia's industry-standard A100 high-performance GPU system.
The human brain contains billions of neurons packed within the limited space of the skull, maximizing its surface area through an intricate network of folds and grooves. Conventional von Neumann computer architecture separates processors (CPUs and GPUs) from memory, forcing data to shuttle continuously between the two during computation. This creates significant latency and power consumption, particularly when processing massive brain-structure datasets over extended periods. As a result, real-time rendering of fine neural surface structures has traditionally required server infrastructure costing hundreds of millions of dollars.
The Chinese research team overcame this bottleneck by directly embedding a neurodynamics system into a next-generation memory array. More notably, the researchers transformed what had long been regarded as a critical weakness of phase-change memristors—a next-generation memory technology—into a computational advantage. Rather than treating conductance drift, or fluctuations in electrical current over time that destabilize stored data, as a flaw, they leveraged the phenomenon to perform highly precise calculations on continuously changing brain signals. In a commentary published in Science, leading scholars at Germany's Jülich Research Centre praised the achievement, comparing China's new memory paradigm to "processing fresh milk directly at a dairy farm instead of repeatedly transporting crude oil to a distant refinery," highlighting its fundamentally different approach to computing efficiency.
Research Controls and Patent Offensive Mirror Strategies of Technology Leaders
Perhaps more striking is China's growing adoption of strategies long employed by leading technology powers such as the United States. Whereas Chinese researchers previously focused on publishing papers in leading international journals to gain global recognition, Beijing has increasingly shifted toward preventing the overseas disclosure of critical technologies. According to the Financial Times, the Chinese government is considering reducing or eliminating the additional credit historically awarded to university faculty and researchers for publishing papers in prestigious international journals. Chinese academics have traditionally received advantages in hiring, promotions, and research funding evaluations for publishing in journals such as Nature and Cell. However, growing concerns that academic publications could serve as channels for industrial and technological leakage have prompted authorities to consider tightening restrictions on overseas journal submissions.
Beijing has already strengthened oversight of overseas academic publishing since August of last year while encouraging researchers to publish influential work in domestic journals instead. articles.title: Why South Korea’s KOSPI Is Crushing Global Stocks - Cabot Wealth Network
articles.summary: Why South Korea’s KOSPI Is Crushing Global Stocks  Cabot Wealth Network

For most investors, 2026 has been yet another feather in the cap of U.S. equities. The S&P 500 continues to push higher, the Nasdaq just hit another all-time high, artificial intelligence remains the defining investment theme, and mega-cap technology companies are at the helm.
But while Wall Street has dominated the discourse, the performance of U.S. equities has been massively outshone by one global stock market index: South Korea’s KOSPI index.
And the headlines touting that outperformance have been few and far between.
That’s partly because of what behavioral economists call home country bias – the tendency for investors to overwhelmingly favor stocks from their own country, even when compelling opportunities exist elsewhere. U.S. investors are particularly susceptible because American markets have outperformed for so long and because the U.S. market is already home to many of the world’s largest companies.
But that blind spot, which leads investors to eschew global markets in favor of domestic markets, can be a costly mistake.
Case in point: The KOSPI has been the best-performing global index over the last year, fueled largely by an explosion in demand for semiconductors and AI-related hardware. In 2026 alone, the KOSPI has surged 64.3%, which has helped drive the index an astronomical 103.9% higher in the last 12 months.
[text_ad]
Why the KOSPI Has Been So Strong
South Korea sits at the center of one of the most important investment trends in the world: artificial intelligence infrastructure.
The country is home to semiconductor giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix (SKHY), two critical suppliers of memory chips powering AI servers, data centers, and next-generation computing systems. As demand for AI infrastructure has surged globally, Korean chipmakers have become major beneficiaries.
The Important Caveat: This Is a Narrow Market
U.S. investors have become pretty comfortable investing in a narrow market.
To wit: From the end of March until mid-May, 10 stocks were responsible for 69% of the U.S. market’s recent gains, and the 10 largest companies in the U.S. now account for 37.8% of the total market cap of the S&P 500. But the KOSPI takes that market concentration to a whole new level.
The index is heavily dominated by (and the recent performance has primarily been driven by) the two aforementioned chipmakers.
The iShares MSCI South Korea ETF (EWY), which tracks the KOSPI (and is one of the most accessible ways for U.S. investors to add Korean exposure), is heavily concentrated in SK Hynix and Samsung.
As of September 22, SK Hynix represents 22.5% of the fund’s assets, just behind Samsung’s 22.9% share.
In other words, just two companies command more than 45% of the total value of the index.
That concentration has amplified gains during the AI boom, but it also creates significant volatility any time the AI trade falls out of favor and can lead to sharp downside moves.
From the end of March through the end of May, EWY boomed 77%, with multiple 5%+ days along the way. But that volatility cuts both ways, and the fund experienced multiple one-day crashes over the summer, including declines of 14% (June 5) and 12% (June 23).
Another practical issue is accessibility.
Aside from SK Hynix, which listed its ADRs in the U.S. earlier this year, buying individual South Korean stocks directly can be difficult for U.S.-based investors, which keeps many investors from exploring global opportunities.
And, given the strength of U.S. equities, the opportunity cost of missing the global trade has been muted by strong performance at home.
Should You Buy the EWY?
So, given the incredible performance and heightened risk, the million-dollar question is: Should investors consider adding Korean exposure via EWY?
Yes… but with a healthy dose of skepticism.
Buying EWY gives you representative exposure to the KOSPI, both the upside and downside, and your results will be dictated by the performance of Samsung and SK Hynix.
In fact, because Samsung has been such a disproportionately large piece of the Korean stock market for many years, EWY has often been a way for U.S. investors to indirectly build stakes in that company.
In other words, buying EWY is a play on Samsung and SK Hynix, with little consideration given to the rest of the Korean market.
So, if you want to invest in those two particular South Korean tech companies, EWY is a good way to do it, just don’t expect the same level of risk as a broadly diversified international fund.
A Final Note on International Investing
For years, many investors have become increasingly concentrated in U.S. assets because that strategy has worked extraordinarily well. But markets move in cycles. Leadership rotates. Entire countries and sectors can spend years ignored before suddenly becoming market leaders.
Carl Delfeld, Chief Analyst of Cabot Explorer, has written about investment concentration in the U.S. and the inevitable reallocation towards the rest of the world, a phenomenon he refers to as the “Great Rebalancing.”
And while the KOSPI bull market may be unique due to the high weights of Samsung and SK Hynix, large-scale capital flows to high-potential international markets are not.

North Korea has emphatically rejected renewed diplomatic efforts to curb its nuclear programme, with a senior diplomat dismissing the prospect of denuclearisation as an "unrealistic delusion" and declaring the country's atomic arsenal "irreversible." The stark rebuke directly answers recent overtures from Seoul and a trilateral summit involving the United States, South Korea, and Japan, signaling a hardening of Pyongyang's posture just as Washington and its allies attempt to revive stalled negotiations.
Foreign Minister Choe Son Hui issued the definitive statement via state-run media, reaffirming the regime's commitment to maintaining its nuclear deterrent through all ages. The declaration effectively shuts the door on phased arms-control proposals recently floated by South Korean leadership, setting the stage for continued geopolitical friction on the Korean Peninsula.
The Irreversible Doctrine
Choe Son Hui's statement was a direct response to a trilateral meeting between the United States, South Korea, and Japan, where the three nations reaffirmed their commitment to the complete denuclearisation of North Korea. Pyongyang has long maintained that its nuclear status is non-negotiable, but the recent rhetoric underscores a deliberate strategy to normalize its position as a nuclear-armed state in international discourse.
"I reaffirm and reconfirm in the strongest tone of voice the steadfast will of our state to keep nuclear weapons through all ages," Choe stated, adding that the country’s nuclear status was "irreversible in any case and will remain unchanged forever." She warned that the more Washington and its allies pushed for denuclearisation, the harder Pyongyang’s position would become, framing international pressure as justification for further arsenal expansion.
Seoul's Phased Freeze Proposal
The North Korean dismissal lands just as South Korean President Lee Jae Myung attempts to shift the diplomatic paradigm. In a recent interview, Lee argued that demanding complete denuclearisation under current circumstances would achieve little, given Pyongyang’s continued expansion of its nuclear capabilities. He proposed a phased approach, suggesting the United States consider offering sanctions relief in return for North Korea freezing the development of additional nuclear weapons and intercontinental ballistic missile technology.
Lee has warned that North Korea may now be capable of producing an additional 10 to 20 nuclear weapons annually. He cautioned that continued expansion could eventually create incentives for Pyongyang to export nuclear weapons and missile technology for financial gain, posing a severe proliferation risk to the broader international community. Despite these warnings, Pyongyang's latest statement indicates zero appetite for even a temporary freeze.
The Trump Factor and Continued Testing
South Korean leadership has also pointed to US President Donald Trump’s previous engagements with Kim Jong Un as a potential opening for renewed diplomacy. Trump met the North Korean leader three times during his first term and has indicated plans to meet him again later this year. Lee noted that Trump "clearly wants dialogue" with Pyongyang, hoping that personal diplomacy might bypass the entrenched bureaucratic stalemate.
However, North Korea has continued its weapons development unabated, regardless of signals from Washington or Seoul. Just days before the latest statement, Pyongyang announced the successful testing of "updated 240-millimetre controlled multiple-launch rockets" capable of striking targets up to 115 kilometres away. The regime also recently rejected an International Atomic Energy Agency resolution criticizing its nuclear programme, further isolating itself from global non-proliferation norms.
Strategic Implications for the Peninsula
The entrenchment of North Korea's nuclear doctrine presents a profound challenge for regional security architecture. With dialogue stalled and arms control proposals rejected, the United States and its allies are left with limited options beyond enhanced deterrence and stricter sanctions enforcement. The failure of the phased freeze proposal suggests that Pyongyang views any concession on its weapons programme as an existential threat, regardless of the economic incentives offered.
As North Korea continues to refine its delivery systems and expand its fissile material stockpiles, the prospect of a denuclearised peninsula appears increasingly distant. The international community now faces the reality of managing a permanent nuclear-armed North Korea, requiring new strategies for containment, crisis communication, and deterrence in an increasingly volatile region.

AI Semiconductor Demand Fuels Export Growth  
Korea’s GDP Growth Forecast for Next Year Raised to 2.3%, Up by 0.3 Points
    The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has revised its economic growth forecast for South Korea this year upward to 3.2%. This adjustment reflects increased exports driven by growing global demand for artificial intelligence (AI) semiconductors and a recovery in private consumption as corporate performance improves.
On September 23, in its newly released "Asian Economic Outlook," the ADB projected South Korea's real GDP growth rate this year at 3.2%. This figure is 0.6 percentage points higher than the 2.6% presented in the July supplementary outlook, and 1.3 percentage points higher than the 1.9% forecast released in April. The ADB's forecast for Korea's growth this year is similar to projections made by major domestic institutions. Last month, the Bank of Korea raised its outlook from 2.6% to 3.3%. The Korea Development Institute (KDI) expects 3.2%, the government projects 3.0%, and international credit rating agency Moody's forecasts 3.5%.
President Donald Trump signed a proclamation imposing a 25% tariff without exceptions on steel and aluminum products imported into the United States and announced that tariffs on automobiles and semiconductors are also under consideration. On February 13, 2025, export vehicles and containers are waiting to be loaded at Pyeongtaek Port, Gyeonggi Province. Photo by Kang Jinhyung

The ADB cited robust manufacturing indicators in July and August, as well as increased exports due to rising global AI semiconductor demand, as major reasons for the upward revision. The bank also expects private consumption to recover moderately, backed by expansionary fiscal policies and improved corporate earnings. In fact, strong semiconductor exports are serving as a key driver behind Korea's outperformance this year. Previously, the Bank of Korea also raised its growth outlook, viewing the surge in semiconductor-centered exports as offsetting downward pressures on growth. According to the Korea Customs Service, semiconductor exports from September 1–20 totaled $34.1 billion, an increase of 259.4% year-on-year—a record for this period.
The ADB also upgraded its economic growth forecast for South Korea next year to 2.3%, up from the previous 2.0%, and 0.4 percentage points higher than its April forecast of 1.9%. articles.summary: South Korea's President Lee Jae-myung Turns "AI-Energy Convergence" Vision into Reality Within a Year — Blueprint Unveiled at SEP 2026  finance.biggo.com
articles.full_text:
South Korean President Lee Jae-myung's vision of "combining AI (artificial intelligence) with the energy power grid," first articulated last October, has translated into concrete policy and industry momentum within a single year. The South Korean government has formalized three mega-projects backed by approximately 2,000 trillion won (approximately $1.5 trillion) over ten years, while major South Korean companies are rolling out energy transition strategies centered on AI data centers, next-generation memory, and physical AI.
President Lee first unveiled the concept in his congratulatory address at Smart Energy Plus (SEP) 2025, held on October 15 last year at COEX in Samseong-dong, Seoul, where he declared, "We will combine AI with the energy power grid to create new engines of economic growth." The remarks encapsulated his core governing philosophy, which has consistently emphasized climate crisis response and the transition to a renewable energy-centered society.
The vision was rapidly translated into government policy this year. At his first Blue House senior staff meeting of the year, President Lee framed the AI transformation as "a factor that determines the fate of the nation, beyond individual companies," and directed officials to accelerate talent acquisition, infrastructure expansion, and global cooperation. In June, the government formalized mega-projects built on three pillars: semiconductors, physical AI, and AI data centers. The strategy calls for investing approximately 2,000 trillion won (approximately $1.5 trillion) over ten years to secure irreplaceable competitiveness in advanced technologies.
In August, during policy briefings from the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy and the Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment, President Lee urged officials to "accelerate the delivery of results for South Korea's leap toward becoming an energy powerhouse with super-gap industries," emphasizing the importance of stable power and water supply.
SEP 2026: A Blueprint for the AI-Era Energy Transition
SEP 2026, scheduled for the 28th through the 30th of next month at Hall B of COEX in Seoul, is expected to showcase how this policy direction is being implemented on the ground across South Korean industry. The event's themes are "Energy Transition in the AI Era" and "Energy Security Amid a Rapidly Shifting International Landscape."
On the second day, the 29th, presentations on energy transition in the AI revolution era will be delivered by Han Jae-joon, Senior Vice President and Master of Samsung Electronics' AX·PI Center; Choi Jun-yong, Vice President in charge of HBM business planning at SK Hynix; Kim Young-hoon, Head of Hyundai Motor's Robotics Lab; Yoon Il-yong, Director of POSCO Holdings' Future Technology Research Center; Lee Kwang-won of LG Electronics; and Kim Hee-sung, Chairman of Bright Energy Partners.
On the third day, Kim Hyun-tae, Senior Vice President at LG Energy Solution; Hyun Jang-seok, Senior Vice President at Samsung SDI; Choi Dae-jin, Head of Division at SK On; Kim Sung-yup, CEO of OCI Power; and Ok Kyung-seok, Senior Vice President at HD Hyundai Electric, will discuss opportunities to participate in the "AI gold rush." LG Group, HD Hyundai Electric, Doosan Enerbility, and Unison will operate exhibition booths focused on energy security strategies for the AI era.
On the first day, the South Korean Army will host an "Energy Policy Forum" on military energy transition for climate crisis response and national energy security. The Army will also exhibit a microgrid system that stores solar-generated electricity in ESS (Energy Storage Systems) for use when needed, supplemented by diesel generators when generation falls short.
From Fast Follower to First Mover
The Herald Business Forum 2026, held the same day at the Shilla Hotel in Seoul, also placed AI-centered economic paradigm shift at the top of its agenda. Now in its tenth year, the forum drew approximately 600 attendees under the theme "Beyond Follower: Transition to a First-Mover Economy."
In a congratulatory message read on his behalf by Sung Ki-hong, Senior Presidential Secretary for Public Communication, President Lee diagnosed that "the past 'fast follower' growth strategy of rapidly adopting and refining advanced technologies is no longer valid." He added, "To become a leader in the global economy and enjoy limitless opportunities, we must boldly integrate AI into industrial settings and build a robust ecosystem."
In his keynote address, Chung Eun-seung, Advisor at Samsung Electronics, emphasized that future competitiveness will stem from "comprehensive innovation capabilities that connect memory, logic, foundry, and packaging." He added that such innovation is achievable not in isolation, but through trust-based collaboration with customers, universities, research institutes, and materials and equipment companies.
Lee Jae-wook, Professor of Computer Science and Engineering and Director of Seoul National University's AI Research Institute, assessed that South Korea stands at a crossroads between being a "components nation" and a "full-stack nation," stressing that "trust between institutions, within organizations, and between humans and AI is the most critical fuel."
In the semiconductor session, Kim Kyung-ryun, Senior Vice President of Samsung Electronics' DRAM Development Office, unveiled "zHBM," a 3D memory architecture that transcends the limitations of existing 2.5D structures, charting the evolution path for next-generation High Bandwidth Memory (HBM). Lim Eui-chul, Vice President at SK Hynix, emphasized that the emergence of AI inference models and agentic AI is further amplifying the importance of memory.
Kwon Seok-joon, Associate Dean of Sungkyunkwan University's College of Engineering, cautioned that "the memory supercycle does not permit unconditional optimism," recommending a path forward through memory-systems co-design, public fab and ecosystem strengthening, manufacturing AI transformation, and the integration of energy and semiconductor security.
In the physical AI session, Chung Joon-chul, President of Hyundai Motor and Kia's Manufacturing Division, presented a vision for "autonomous operating factories" where humans and robots collaborate. Hyun Jang-seok, Senior Vice President at Samsung SDI, introduced cylindrical cells and solid-state technology for humanoids, emphasizing that batteries are the "heart" of the physical AI era. Kim Young-ok, Chief AI Officer at HD Hyundai, outlined the direction for South Korean manufacturing AI based on the company's manufacturing AI transformation case studies.
The Triangular Axis of Energy, Semiconductors, and AI
A common thread running through both the forum and SEP 2026 is the recognition that sustainable growth in the AI industry is impossible without energy transition. As power demand from AI data centers surges, stable electricity supply and expanded renewable energy are emerging as prerequisites for AI competitiveness.
The government's three mega-projects are likewise structured so that the three pillars of semiconductors, physical AI, and AI data centers are underpinned by the energy transition. President Lee's vision of "combining AI with the energy power grid," first articulated at SEP 2025 last year, has effectively become the central axis of South Korean industrial policy within a single year.
The concrete energy security strategies and technology roadmaps that major South Korean companies will unveil at SEP 2026 next month are expected to serve as a bellwether for the direction of South Korea's AI and energy policy over the coming year.

articles.title: 'South Jeolla-Gwangju can become Korea's Shenzhen': Samsung advisor urges semiconductor push [Herald Business Forum 2026] - 헤럴드경제
articles.summary: 'South Jeolla-Gwangju can become Korea's Shenzhen': Samsung advisor urges semiconductor push [Herald Business Forum 2026]  헤럴드경제
articles.full_text:
Keynote address by Jung Eun-seung, Samsung Electronics advisor
Speed emphasized for fabs in Yongin, Icheon and South Jeolla-Gwangju
Supply shortages driving price volatility
Semiconductors described as core technology enabling human imagination
Samsung Electronics must create its own 'inflection point' to reclaim global leadership
"South Jeolla-Gwangju, with a population of 3.2 million, can transform into a city like Shenzhen — China's big-tech hub of about 18 million people. To build that kind of city 30 years from now, the semiconductor industry must take root here."
Jung Eun-seung, an advisor to Samsung Electronics, drew a parallel Tuesday between Samsung's own entry into the semiconductor business and the vision for building a semiconductor industry in the newly integrated South Jeolla-Gwangju Special City. Speaking at the Herald Business Forum 2026 at the Dynasty Hall of Shilla Hotel in Jung-gu, Seoul, he said the goal is not to chase opportunities that have already been proven, but to create the inflection points that open new ones.
Jung took on the role of transition committee chair after Mayor-elect Min Hyeong-bae won the South Jeolla-Gwangju Integrated Special City election in June. He later became chair of the city's semiconductor strategy committee as a semiconductor mega-project began to give concrete shape to investment plans for the southwestern region.
"I asked Mayor Min why he was calling on me — a position that usually goes to a university president," Jung said. "He told me he wanted to do for South Jeolla-Gwangju what semiconductors had done for Korea's industrial growth."
He said that given an industrial structure in which nothing is now possible without semiconductors, every region — including South Jeolla-Gwangju — must accelerate semiconductor investment without delay.
"The reason Nvidia's GPUs are so expensive is that supply still covers only 60 to 70 percent of what AI companies want — the shortage is that severe," Jung said. "The same is true of the HBM that Samsung Electronics and SK hynix produce." He added that whenever he meets anyone connected to the semiconductor industry, his message is the same: build the factories in Yongin, Icheon and South Jeolla-Gwangju as fast as possible.
He said price volatility, too, is a problem that will ease once supply stabilizes. "Right now, prices are surging because there isn't enough supply, and the market swings wildly even when it looks like there's a surplus," he said, stressing the need to expand the supply base.
Jung described semiconductors as the core technology that makes human imagination possible, citing the film "2001: A Space Odyssey" as an example. The 1968 film featured scenes evoking AI, video calls and tablet computers — ideas that were pure fantasy at the time but have since become reality. "I believe everything you can imagine will come true," he said, "and semiconductor technology is the foundation that makes it possible."
He saw the position Korean companies have secured in memory chips as a springboard for new opportunities. "The fact that we pulled off memory is what has given us the chance to play an important role on the world stage," Jung said. "We have to make the most of that opportunity."
The word Jung returned to most often throughout his presentation was "inflection point." Reflecting on the period when Samsung Electronics first entered the memory chip business, he said: "There are no ready-made opportunities in the world. An inflection point is something you find and create out of nothing."
"When Samsung started in semiconductors, nobody knew it would work," he said, adding that the industry's competitive strength today was not gained by following existing markets.
He said the same approach had worked in technology development, citing efforts such as increasing wafer sizes and converting NAND flash from a planar to a three-dimensional structure.
On 3D NAND, he said the breakthrough combined "innovation in materials, innovation in structure, and innovation in integration technology" — the product of years of research and a true technological inflection point.
He also argued that making individual chips well is no longer sufficient on its own. "We have moved from selling discrete components to selling integrated products like SSDs and HBM," Jung said, adding that new opportunities must be found at the intersection of memory, foundry and packaging. He also pointed to combining technology with software to raise the value that semiconductors deliver.
He identified collaboration and trust as essential conditions for that journey. Drawing on his experience co-developing technology with global companies, he said: "I never knew trust could be such a powerful word in business." The point, he explained, is that partners must believe you will stay the course even when times are hard.
He also shared an anecdote involving Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. When Samsung Electronics was set to take on production of Nvidia's 8-nanometer GPU, a marketing executive told Huang, "We're in the same boat." Huang pushed back. "If we're in the same boat, that means you can swim away when things get dangerous," Huang said. "We're in the same spaceship." Jung cited the exchange to underscore the sense of urgency that business partnerships demand.
He also shared lessons from the organizational culture he absorbed at Samsung Electronics — mantras he said he returned to whenever things got difficult: "Set big goals," "Give more than you think is necessary," and "Understand everything in numbers."
"When you give everything you have, your teammates are moved by it, and that energy is what gets you through the hardest challenges," Jung said. "Don't waste time talking to people who only say it can't be done. When people believe something is possible, they come up with the ideas that make it happen."
Jung said the next chapter of the semiconductor industry will also be opened through new challenges. "Now, only the best will have a chance to survive," he said, stressing that both business and technology must reach their own inflection points.

articles.title: Lee Warns North Korea May Export Nuclear Weapons Once Stockpiles Grow - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: Lee Warns North Korea May Export Nuclear Weapons Once Stockpiles Grow  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
NEW YORK — President Lee Jae-myung said on the 21st that "trading away sanctions that have little practical effect in exchange for a halt to further nuclear weapons and intercontinental ballistic missile technology development would be of considerable value." The remark laid out a realistic path within his phased denuclearization concept of freeze, reduction and dismantlement.
Lee, who is in New York for the U.N. General Assembly, said in a New York Times interview published that day that "if we set denuclearization as the goal under the current circumstances, we will achieve nothing." Behind the comment is a view that easing sanctions is the realistic way to curb North Korea's nuclear weapons and ICBMs, given the country's changed international standing as it draws closer to Russia and China.
Lee also warned of proliferation risks. "North Korea currently has the capacity to produce an additional 10 to 20 nuclear weapons each year," he said. "If it judges that it has secured enough nuclear weapons and missiles, it will be tempted to export them to make money." He added that "that would be a truly dangerous moment."
On talks between Washington and Pyongyang, Lee made his support clear, asking "what option is left other than diplomacy." In a written interview with The Associated Press released the same day, he said that "both South Korea and the United States are willing to talk with North Korea without preconditions," stressing that "what is needed now is a political decision at the leaders' level."
Asked about U.S. President Donald Trump's criticism over investment negotiations with Washington, Lee said he "fully understands that the U.S. president can make various remarks from his position." He also said that "sending troops to a war between third countries is prohibited by the Constitution of the Republic of Korea," adding that he is "not shaken" by pressure to deploy forces to the Strait of Hormuz.
Separately, Lee approved the appointments of Lee Hyoung-il as deputy prime minister and minister of finance and economy, Kang Shin-chul as defense minister and Hong Ji-sun as land minister immediately after arriving in the United States. The presidential office also expressed "deep regret" over Supreme Court Chief Justice Jo Hee-de's refusal to renominate a Supreme Court justice.
Lee: Trade Sanctions Relief for Halt to Nuclear Weapons, ICBMs
Lee's decision to raise the possibility that North Korea could export nuclear weapons abroad is read as an attempt to alert the international community that the North's nuclear program could spill beyond the Korean Peninsula into a global proliferation threat. Also at work was a sense of urgency that pursuing only "complete denuclearization" while the North keeps expanding its arsenal would mean "achieving nothing."
In the New York Times interview published on the 21st, Lee said that "if North Korea judges that it has secured enough nuclear weapons and missiles to guarantee its own survival, it will fall to the temptation of exporting them to make money," adding that "that would be a truly dangerous moment." The warning suggests Seoul must now consider not only the North's pursuit of deterrence for regime survival but the prospect of it spreading nuclear weapons outward.
The comments also rest on a judgment that the international landscape around North Korea has shifted. Since the war between Russia and Ukraine began, the North has supplied troops and weapons to Russia, and both Russia and China have again embraced it as a strategic partner. The New York Times assessed that the war in Ukraine and the U.S. strikes on Iran have further hardened the North's determination to expand its nuclear deterrent. In other words, isolation and sanctions alone no longer suffice to bring Pyongyang to the negotiating table as they once might have.
Lee's remark that "if we set denuclearization as the goal under the current circumstances, we will achieve nothing" reflects that context. Rather than abandoning eventual denuclearization, he argues for first breaking the vicious cycle in which the North's nuclear capability keeps growing while complete dismantlement is demanded as the starting point for talks.
In the AP interview released the same day, Lee spelled out his solution as freeze, then reduction, then dismantlement. "To change the direction of a moving car, you first have to bring it to a stop," he said, calling the phased approach "a practical way to effectively resolve the North Korean nuclear issue." He plans to present the same phased, practical approach in his keynote address to the U.N. General Assembly on the 23rd.
As a corresponding step to secure a freeze first, he put sanctions relief on the table. Lee told the New York Times that "trading away sanctions that have little practical effect in exchange for a halt to further nuclear weapons and intercontinental ballistic missile technology development would be of considerable value."
In an interview with Time marking his 100th day in office last year, he had gone only as far as leaving open the possibility that "compensation could be offered." This time he went a step further, presenting a concrete corresponding measure that would swap a halt to nuclear and ICBM development for sanctions relief. The idea is to offer Pyongyang incentives, build trust and ultimately create conditions in which it concludes it can survive without nuclear weapons.
Whether phased denuclearization can succeed is a separate question. Lee Kyu-jung, a research professor at Korea University's Institute for Peace and Democracy, said that "in the end, how tightly verification and corresponding measures are designed in the process leading from a nuclear freeze to reduction and dismantlement will determine whether the phased denuclearization concept succeeds or fails." The AP also noted concerns that the North could obtain what it wants, such as sanctions relief, in return for giving up part of its nuclear capability and then refuse full disarmament.
Lee also voiced expectations for Trump's role in that process. Trump has himself shown interest in resuming summit diplomacy with Pyongyang, emphasizing his "very good relationship" with leader Kim. "The two leaders need to build trust, meet directly and find common ground," Lee said, reiterating that "what is needed now is a political decision at the leaders' level." He also assessed positively Trump's signals of willingness to resume talks with the North, including scaled-back South Korea-U.S. joint military exercises, calling them "a deliberate step to send a clear message that the United States has no hostile intent toward North Korea."
At the same time, Lee took a measured tone toward U.S. pressure over investment in the United States and a troop deployment to the Strait of Hormuz. On Trump's series of remarks, he said he "fully understands that the U.S. president can make various statements from his position," and on the Hormuz deployment he reaffirmed his existing position that it is "difficult under the South Korean Constitution."
Even so, he stressed that he "plans to build a more reciprocal alliance during the remainder of President Trump's term." Citing shipbuilding cooperation as an example, he said such work "can revive U.S. shipbuilding and naval power while also offering new growth opportunities to South Korean companies."
